text.headline: Automotive Security Timeline
text.text:
The "Automotive Security Timeline" is an open-source connected vehicle security knowledge base that continuously catalogs important events, vulnerability disclosures, security research, and security incident reports related to global automotive cybersecurity. It organizes scattered information into a unified timeline view, helping researchers, engineers, and security analysts quickly understand the development context of automotive security and emerging threat trends.

Project URL: Automotive Security Timeline

Contact email: delikely@gmail.com

media.caption: Personal Information of 100,000 Citroen Owners May Be Leaked

text.headline: Personal Information of 100,000 Citroen Owners May Be Leaked
text.text: According to Consumer Reports, a hacker with the online alias "Brother Cat" was selling car owner information on the internet. "Brother Cat" provided screenshots of the database. The screenshots showed 15 order records from 7 cities, including car owner names, mobile phone numbers, and intended vehicle models for purchase. The order times were concentrated after 8 PM on May 4, 2015, with the most recent order having occurred just 5 minutes prior. The data screenshot provided by the hacker "Brother Cat" showed that there were 540,676 additional records, with 100,000 non-duplicate pre-sale records. As for the source of the data, the hacker "Brother Cat" attributed it to "laziness" — Dongfeng Citroen essentially neglected its backend, which was the main reason the data could be easily obtained.

media.caption: Hackers Remotely Kill a Jeep on the Highway—With Me in It

text.headline: Jeep and Chrysler Can Be Remotely Hijacked, Chrysler Recalls 1.4 Million Cars and Trucks
text.text: Due to concerns about hackers controlling vehicles, Chrysler announced a recall of 1.4 million cars and trucks. In a demonstration by two hackers, they proved that critical vehicle function controls could be remotely accessed from anywhere with internet connectivity, such as applying the brakes, killing the engine, driving the vehicle off the road, and causing all electronic devices to crash.

media.caption: OwnStar: Unlock and track any GM OnStar connected car for $100

text.headline: General Motors OnStar System Has Security Vulnerability
text.text: Security researcher Samy Kamkar discovered a vulnerability in the OnStar in-vehicle system that could be used to control General Motors vehicles, enabling remote unlocking and engine starting. By intercepting the communication between the OnStar system and the OnStar application on the car owner's phone, the researcher used a self-made OwnStar device to hijack the data communication of the OnStar companion app RemoteLink. OwnStar intercepts the data communication between the vehicle and the mobile app, and sends specific data packets to the target device. These malicious data packets exploit a privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain high-privilege user credentials, after which OwnStar can retrieve vehicle information and even remotely control the vehicle.

media.caption: Guifu Lab of Myth Operation Team: A Research on Defects in Automotive Anti-Theft Systems

text.headline: Volvo, BYD, and Buick Regal Door Lock Remote Control Rolling Code Mechanism Bypassed
text.text:
The Guifu Lab of the "Myth Operation" team discovered design flaws in the anti-theft systems of certain vehicles from Volvo, BYD, and Buick. The remote control rolling code mechanism could be bypassed, allowing car doors and trunks to be opened an unlimited number of times using a cracking key costing only tens of yuan.

Guifu Lab targeted automotive remote control anti-theft systems based on mainstream HCS rolling code chips and the Keeloq algorithm. By eavesdropping on (not intercepting) the wireless remote control data signals from the car's remote key, and replaying the captured signals according to a specific mechanism, they successfully achieved unlimited reproduction of the car remote key's functionality, thereby bypassing the vehicle's security system. This flaw requires manufacturers to recall vehicles for upgrade and repair (if upgradeable), and ordinary users have essentially no means of defense. This flaw was publicly disclosed for the first time.

media.caption: Controlling vehicle features of Nissan LEAFs across the globe via vulnerable APIs

text.headline: Controlling Air Conditioning via Unauthorized WEB API and IDOR Vulnerability in Nissan Leaf Mobile Application
text.text:
Security researcher Troy Hunt found that the Nissan Leaf electric vehicle was vulnerable to attacks, allowing attackers to control the vehicle's air conditioning. The NissanConnect application API lacked authentication verification — requests without any authentication session value could still be successfully executed. The vehicle control requests used the VIN code as the identifier for the target vehicle. By replacing the VIN with another vehicle's VIN, an attacker could gain control of other vehicles, such as retrieving air conditioning status information and controlling the air conditioning. However, car doors could not be opened, as the Nissan Leaf does not support remote door unlocking via the mobile application.

POC: Turn on air conditioning
GET https://[redacted].com/orchestration_1111/gdc/ACRemoteRequest.php?RegionCode=NE&lg=no-NO&DCMID=&VIN=SJNFAAZE0U60XXXXX&tz=Europe/Paris

POC: Turn off air conditioning
GET https://[redacted].com/orchestration_1111/gdc/ACRemoteOffRequest.php?RegionCode=NE&lg=no-NO&DCMID=&VIN=SJNFAAZE0U60XXXXX&tz=Europe/Paris

media.caption: Hacking industrial vehicles from the internet

text.headline: C4Max TGU Misconfigured, Exposed on Public Internet
text.text: The C4Max Telematics Gateway Unit (TGU) manufactured by New Eagle was accessible via a public IP address and port 23 (Telnet) without any authentication. Through Telnet, one could obtain the vehicle's GPS routes, as well as information such as modem network status, vehicle speed, battery voltage, and alarms. It was also possible to set up geofencing restrictions for the vehicle and control the CAN bus.

media.caption: Hacking industrial vehicles from the internet

text.headline: Pen Test Partners Hack Mitsubishi Outlander via Wi-Fi
text.text: Many applications used for vehicle positioning, flashing headlights, remote locking, and other functions use network services from vehicle providers or service providers for remote control. Users control various modules in the vehicle through cellular networks. The Mitsubishi Outlander plug-in hybrid electric vehicle used a different working mechanism. This vehicle was equipped with a Wi-Fi access point instead of a GSM module. Users needed to connect to the hotspot shared by the vehicle to control various module functions. Mitsubishi wrote the Wi-Fi pre-shared key in the user manual, and the format was very short. Therefore, Pen Test Partners took only 4 days to brute-force the key. After obtaining the SSID and the associated PSK, attackers could carry out a series of attacks. Since there was no further authentication after cracking the Wi-Fi PSK, researchers could send messages to turn off the vehicle's alarm, turn lights on or off, control the air conditioning, and more. The access point used an SSID in the format REMOTEnnaaaa, where "n" is a digit and "a" is a lowercase letter. Researchers could easily locate Outlander vehicles by searching on wigle.net. This means that car thieves or hackers could also easily find target vehicles.

media.caption: BMW - (Token) Cross Site Scripting Web Vulnerability

text.headline: Hackers Can Tamper with BMW Vehicle Settings via BMW Portal Vulnerabilities
text.text:
ConnectedDrive is a "connected driving" service jointly developed by German company BMW and Google in 2006, and is also the name of BMW's in-vehicle infotainment system. This system can be used in-vehicle or through a series of connected mobile applications that allow drivers to manage vehicle settings via mobile devices. In addition to the mobile applications, the service also has a web version.
Security researcher Benjamin Kunz Mejri from Vulnerability Lab disclosed two zero-day vulnerabilities in the ConnectedDrive portal, which BMW had left unpatched for 5 months.

Vulnerability 1: VIN Session Hijacking
The session vulnerability allowed a user to access another user's VIN. The VIN is the vehicle ID for each user account. The VIN code backs up the vehicle's ConnectedDrive settings to the user's account. Changing these settings on the portal would modify the in-vehicle settings as well as the companion application. Mejri stated that he could bypass VIN session authentication and use another VIN to access and modify another user's vehicle settings. The ConnectedDrive portal settings include locking/unlocking the vehicle, managing song playlists, accessing email accounts, managing routes, obtaining real-time traffic information, and more.
POC: https://www.bmw-connecteddrive.co.uk/cdp/release/internet/servlet/vehicle?vin=

Vulnerability 2: XSS on the ConnectedDrive Portal
The portal's password reset page contained an XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) vulnerability. This XSS vulnerability could enable network attacks such as browser cookie theft, subsequent Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), and phishing attacks. Mejri claimed that he reported both vulnerabilities to BMW in February 2016. Since BMW did not respond to Mejri's vulnerability report in a timely manner, Mejri publicly disclosed the vulnerabilities.
POC: https://www.bmw.de/de/publicPools/landingPages/passwordResetOk.html?t=OiWU9ARpVXDXDjlRJ3tS6XxgnOvkFzRK%22%3E%3C[CLIENT SIDE SCRIPT CODE INJECT!]iframe%20src=a%20onload=alert%28document.cookie%29%20%3C

media.caption: A Security Analysis of an In-Vehicle Infotainment and App Platform

text.headline: MirrorLink Buffer Overflow Vulnerability
text.text:
Damon McCoy, Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at New York University Tandon School of Engineering, along with students from George Mason University, discovered the MirrorLink vulnerability. MirrorLink is a "connected vehicle" standard jointly initiated by several internationally renowned mobile phone manufacturers and automakers, aimed at standardizing the effective connection between smartphones and in-vehicle systems to provide a good user experience. When using this standard for phone-to-vehicle interconnection, bidirectional control of specific applications can be achieved between the phone and the vehicle's head unit.

McCoy and his team members found that although MirrorLink was disabled by default, it was relatively easy to enable. This allowed hackers to exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability in MirrorLink to control multiple critical safety components within the vehicle, including the anti-lock braking system (ABS).

media.caption: Intruding into and Damaging Mechanical Remote Monitoring System Constitutes the Crime of Damaging Computer Information Systems

text.headline: Self-Taught Illegal Unlocking of SANY Heavy Industry Pump Trucks Leads to Prison Sentence
text.text:
Since 2008, SANY Heavy Industry had installed the "SANY Construction Machinery Remote Monitoring System" on pump truck equipment sold through "rent-to-sell," "finance lease," and "mortgage sale" arrangements. The standard product sale (lease) contract explicitly stipulated that "if the buyer fails to timely repay the loan or pay the fees in full, the buyer agrees that the seller may take measures including suspending after-sales service, shutting down, and locking the equipment, and any losses arising therefrom shall be borne by the buyer" and "before the buyer has paid all outstanding payments, the ownership of the subject matter under this contract shall belong to the seller." The company headquarters' remote monitoring and maintenance platform then monitored the pump trucks. If a customer was found to be in arrears, the monitoring system would "lock" the equipment. After receiving the "lock" command, the pump truck could still be started and operated, but could only achieve approximately 30% of its normal working efficiency.

Since November 2012, the defendant Liu Hui self-taught the working principles of the SANY Heavy Industry pump truck remote monitoring system. Together with the defendant Zhu Zhaoren, they collected data from locked and unlocked pump trucks, and based on the collected data, developed a program to unlock the remote monitoring system's vehicle locking mechanism. Subsequently, the two agreed that defendant Zhu Zhaoren would write the unlocking program and produce it as a "microcomputer" (technically named "analog generator," also known as "black box"). Defendant Liu Hui purchased these "microcomputers" at a price of 450-500 yuan each and used them to "unlock" pump trucks for users for profit. By the time of the incident, defendant Zhu Zhaoren had produced over 200 "microcomputers" for unlocking locked pump trucks and sold them to defendant Liu Hui, profiting over 100,000 yuan. After purchasing the "microcomputers" made by Zhu Zhaoren, defendant Liu Hui hired multiple people at a monthly salary of 5,000-10,000 yuan to post large amounts of advertisements on the internet, offering unlocking services for pump truck users and purchasers whose equipment had been locked due to outstanding payments, at a price of 10,000-20,000 yuan per unit.

After contacting customers, defendant Liu Hui and others performed unlocking using the following two methods:
1. For SYLD (SANY LCD Display) showing "Application Layer Lock Mode" status: First, the two CAN data cables on the USBCAN (analyzer) were connected to the B218 and B222 wire ports between the pump truck's SYMC (SANY Motion Controller) and SYLD (SANY LCD Display), then unlocking commands were sent via computer software to the SANY Motion Controller to release the lock. Then, the SANY Motion Controller data was collected via the analyzer and written into the "microcomputer's" RAM. Finally, the two CAN cables on the "microcomputer" were connected in parallel with the B218 and B222 wires connecting the SANY mobile terminal and SANY LCD Display, and the CAN data cable of the "SANY ECC System" was disconnected. The program inside the "microcomputer" then simulated sending unlock commands to the SANY Motion Controller, preventing the pump truck from being locked again.
2. For SYLD (SANY LCD Display) showing "Base Layer Lock Mode" status (this mode is a higher-security lock mode in the SANY Construction Machinery Remote Monitoring System, differing from "Application Layer Lock Mode" by adding an additional lock, with all communication commands encrypted): First, a computer was connected to the SANY Motion Controller, and CAN software was used to send unlock IDs at a rate of once every 20 milliseconds, with 10 frames sent each time. Each frame's ID auto-incremented. When over 30,000 frames had been sent, one of the frames would match the system's ID, and the pump truck's locking program would be cracked. Then, following the same method as cracking the "Application Layer Lock Mode," the pump truck was unlocked and freed from control, preventing it from being locked again.

media.caption: Hyundai Blue Link Potential Info Disclosure

text.headline: Hyundai Blue Link Mobile App Information Disclosure
text.text:
The Hyundai Blue Link mobile application had the potential risk of leaking sensitive user and vehicle information, including usernames, passwords, PIN codes, and more. The vulnerability existed in a new log upload feature introduced in December 2016, affecting versions 3.9.4 and 3.9.5, as of March 6, 2017. The Blue Link mobile app transmitted logs via HTTP to http://54.xx.yy.113:8080/LogManager/LogServlet, where the transmitted logs were encrypted and protected using the symmetric key "1986l12Ov09e".

Attackers could obtain the uploaded logs through a man-in-the-middle attack on an unsecured Wi-Fi network, then decrypt them using the hardcoded key, thereby obtaining the car owner's username, password, and other information.

media.caption: 2011 BMW 330i format string vuln

text.headline: BMW 330i 2011 Model Format String DoS Vulnerability (CVE-2017-9212)
text.text: When a BMW 330i connected to a Bluetooth name containing format string specifiers (%c or %x), it would cause the multimedia software to crash.

media.caption: Security flaws affect TCUs used in BMW, Ford, Infiniti, and Nissan vehicles

text.headline: Vulnerabilities in TCUs of Ford, BMW, Infiniti, and Nissan Vehicles Enable Remote Intrusion
text.text:
These three researchers from McAfee — Mickey Shkatov, Jesse Michael, and Oleksandr Bazhaniuk — presented their research findings at the Defcon conference last week. The TCU is essentially a 2G modem, commonly used in modern vehicles for data transmission. Through this module, vehicles can communicate with each other, and web consoles and mobile apps can be used for remote control.
The vulnerabilities affected the S-Gold 2 (PMB 8876) cellular baseband chip. One vulnerability was a buffer overflow in the component processing AT commands in the TCU (vulnerability ID CVE-2017-9647). These commands included AT+STKPROF, AT+XAPP, AT+XLOG, and AT+FNS, many of which were iPhone vulnerabilities that Apple fixed in 2015. However, executing this attack required physical access to the vehicle. The other vulnerability allowed attackers to exploit TMSI (Temporary Mobile Subscriber Identity) to intrude and control memory (vulnerability ID CVE-2017-9633), which could be exploited remotely. In their presentation, the three researchers noted that exploits targeting the vulnerable firmware had been mentioned as early as 2016 in Ralf-Philipp Weinmann's "iOS Hacker's Handbook."
Researcher Mickey Shkatov specifically pointed out that remotely exploiting the vulnerability did not necessarily require a 2G network. One only needed to purchase an open-source 2G base station: "If an attacker sets up a rogue base station (fake base station), the TCU will connect to it, which can trigger the TMSI vulnerability. As long as the TCU is on and searching for a signal, it can be hacked."

media.caption: Exploit

text.headline: CVE-2017-14937 Airbag Vulnerability
text.text:
The airbag deployment algorithm allowed an attacker to cause harm by sending predictable Security Access (SA) messages to the CAN bus. The airbag deployment algorithm had only 256 possible key pairs, and there was no limit on authentication attempts. Furthermore, at least one manufacturer interpreted the ISO 26021 standard as requiring the key to be directly computed (i.e., the other 255 key pairs could not be used). Therefore, after the vehicle was started and traveling at less than 6 km/h, an attacker could access the CAN bus and send a carefully crafted Unified Diagnostic Services (UDS) message to deploy the airbag, creating a risk of injury to passengers.

This vulnerability was exploited by connecting to the OBD connector or the in-vehicle CAN network to send commands. The attack conditions required the vehicle to be ignited and traveling at less than 6 km/h. By obtaining CAN command access and sending UDS service messages to the in-vehicle network via the OBD interface, the attacker could attack the airbag system, potentially causing physical harm to vehicle occupants. This vulnerability affected passenger vehicles manufactured from 2014 onwards.

media.caption: Important Careem Security Information

text.headline: Ride-Hailing Company Careem Attacked, Data Breach Affects 14 Million Users
text.text:
Careem, a Dubai-based ride-hailing company, suffered a cyberattack that resulted in a data breach. The data stolen by hackers included users' names, mobile phone numbers, trip data, and email addresses.

The data breach first occurred in January of this year, so all users who registered with Careem before January 14 were affected by the data breach. However, there was currently no evidence that users' passwords and credit card numbers had been successfully obtained by hackers. Careem also stated that the company discovered the data breach in January of this year, immediately launched an investigation, and strengthened its security systems. The data breach affected 14 million passengers and 558,000 drivers, but the company stated that there was no indication that the leaked data had been misused or used for fraud.

media.caption: The Connected Car:Ways to get unauthorized access and potential implications

text.headline: Volkswagen and Audi In-Vehicle Infotainment System Vulnerabilities
text.text:
After security researchers from Computest examined the infotainment system manufactured by Harman and used in the 2015 Volkswagen Golf GTE and Audi A3 Sportback e-tron, they discovered multiple security vulnerabilities in Volkswagen and Audi vehicles that could allow attackers to launch remote attacks. Attackers were fully capable of executing remote code via the internet, controlling the RCC (Remote Control Center), and sending arbitrary CAN messages. Subsequently, attackers would likely attempt to physically control the vehicle's critical safety components.

The researchers discovered a vulnerability in the Volkswagen in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) system that could be remotely exploited when an attacker connected the vehicle to their own Wi-Fi network. The researchers subsequently found that this vulnerability could also be exploited via the cellular network. Through this vulnerability, researchers could obtain root access to the IVI system's main processor. This processor ran the BlackBerry QNX operating system and was responsible for executing navigation and multimedia decoding functions. Once root access was obtained, researchers could control the RCC or the wireless and vehicle control units, potentially providing a pathway to send malicious messages to the CAN bus, thereby manipulating the vehicle's braking and steering systems.

media.caption: Insider Threat: PLC Source Code Leaked, Nearly One Billion Yuan Worth of SANY Pump Trucks "Disappear"

text.headline: SANY Heavy Industry Technician Tampered with and Deleted Pump Truck Remote Monitoring System, Illegally Unlocking Sold Equipment, Sentenced to Prison
text.text:
Starting from March 2016, SANY Heavy Industry continuously received feedback from branch offices nationwide that multiple sold devices had suddenly lost contact. Upon inspection, SANY Heavy Industry employees discovered that the remote monitoring system (referred to as the ECC system) connecting the equipment had been illegally unlocked and damaged, causing the company to lose control of construction machinery equipment in the field. As time progressed, more and more equipment "disappeared" without explanation, with the number reaching nearly one thousand units.

From 2010 to 2012, Zhang Chao worked at the Control Division of the Concrete Pumping Machinery Division of SANY Heavy Industry Co., Ltd., responsible for writing and debugging pump truck programs. From 2013 to 2015, defendant Zhang Chao worked at the Mixing Equipment Control Division of SANY Heavy Industry, responsible for writing and debugging mixing equipment programs. Taking advantage of his position, Zhang Chao obtained the source program and code of the SYMC (SANY Motion Controller) control program within the SANY Construction Machinery Remote Monitoring System (SANY "ECC" system) installed on pump trucks. After mastering the equipment control principles and code, Zhang Chao modified and deleted the remote locking program in the source code, recompiling it to produce a control program capable of unlocking pump trucks and mixing stations.

Due to the high cost of large construction machinery pump trucks, sales typically involved installment payments. When customers failed to make timely payments, manufacturers could remotely lock the equipment, rendering it inoperable. In the first half of 2016, former SANY Heavy Industry employee Zhou Xiaoping mentioned in a conversation with Zhang Chao that exploiting the company's system vulnerabilities for remote unlocking could yield substantial profits. Tempted by the profits, Zhang Chao agreed to take on the job. Subsequently, Zhang used his position to secretly pass internal materials to Zhou Xiaoping. Afterward, 8 additional members joined the group. Unlocking a device's GPS took less than five minutes, with customer fees ranging from 4,000 to 20,000 yuan. To attract business, the group also registered a WeChat official account for device cracking, used for customer acquisition.

Their actions constituted the crime of damaging computer information systems. The Changsha Intermediate People's Court, in accordance with the Criminal Law and other relevant regulations, imposed combined punishment for two crimes on Zhou Xiaoping, sentencing him to fixed-term imprisonment of four years and six months. For Zhang Chao, combined punishment for two crimes resulted in a fixed-term imprisonment of two years and six months. The remaining 8 men were sentenced to 1-3 years respectively based on the circumstances of their crimes.

media.caption: Hackers Can Steal a Tesla Model S in Seconds by Cloning Its Key Fob

text.headline: Hackers Can Clone Key Fob and Steal Tesla Model S in Seconds (CVE-2018-16806)
text.text: A research team at the University of Leuven in Belgium discovered a security issue in the authentication process between the PKES (Passive Keyless Entry System) and the wireless key fob in the Tesla Model S. Exploiting this security issue, hackers could clone the car key in seconds and steal the vehicle. The Tesla Model S's PKES (DST40 encryption algorithm) was not designed in-house but adopted a solution provided by Pektron. In the authentication process, the wake frame was sent by the vehicle as a low-frequency signal at 134.2 kHz, containing the vehicle's identity information. Since this was a broadcast signal, anyone could capture this wake frame information. The key fob would then reply with a response frame to inform the vehicle-side device that the key was ready for challenge-response authentication at any time. Since the response was only 24 bits, smaller than the 40-bit challenge and key, at least two challenge-response pairs were needed to recover the key. Due to the very small key space and weak mutual authentication mechanism, a Time-Memory Trade-Off attack became possible.

media.caption: Ride-Hailing Driver Uses Charging Station Vulnerability to Steal Electricity in Daxing

text.headline: Ride-Hailing Driver Steals Electricity 382 Times in Six Months Using "Gun Pinch Method" and "Second Card Method", Sentenced to Prison
text.text:
A Beijing ride-hailing driver surnamed Dong exploited vulnerabilities in the State Grid charging software, using the "gun pinch method" and "second card method" to achieve free or low-cost charging, stealing electricity 382 times over a six-month period. The Daxing District People's Procuratorate of Beijing prosecuted Dong for theft and teaching criminal methods, and Dong was sentenced by the court to one year of fixed-term imprisonment and fined 1,000 yuan.

"Gun Pinch Method": Using the e-Charging APP to scan the QR code on the charging station, then paying 0.5 or 1 yuan, waiting a few seconds, and then connecting the charging gun to the electric vehicle. Pressing the switch on the charging gun — if the charging indicator light on the station was lit, it indicated successful electricity theft, and the station would charge the electric vehicle without billing.
"Second Card Method": Using the e-Charging APP to scan the QR code on the charging station, then paying 0.5 or 1 yuan, waiting a few seconds before pressing the charging gun switch plugged into the vehicle. The charging station screen would display the start of billing with a second counter. After waiting 10 seconds, pressing the return button on the screen, then scanning the QR code on the charging station again with the e-Charging APP. If the charging indicator light was lit, it indicated successful electricity theft; otherwise, it meant the theft failed and needed to be retried.

media.caption: Jailbreaking Subaru StarLink

text.headline: FHI Subaru StarLink Harman Head Unit Local Update Verification Flaw (CVE-2018-18203)
text.text: A vulnerability existed in the update mechanism of the Subaru 2017, 2018, and 2019 model StarLink head units, allowing attackers to flash tampered firmware via the vehicle's USB port. This vulnerability was due to a flaw in the signature verification used when validating update files. Attackers could flash malicious head unit firmware and execute arbitrary code with root user privileges.

media.caption: Remotely controlled EV home chargers – the threats and vulnerabilities

text.headline: Multiple Vulnerabilities in ChargePoint Home Charging Station
text.text: Kaspersky discovered multiple vulnerabilities in ChargePoint's home charging station, allowing remote attackers to adjust the charging current and stop the vehicle's charging process at any time, potentially leading to physical damage and economic losses. The home charging station supported Wi-Fi and Bluetooth wireless technologies, and users could remotely control the charging process through mobile applications on iOS and Android platforms. Researchers found that the device's web server had vulnerabilities including certificate security issues and buffer overflow.

media.caption: This hack could take control of your Ford

text.headline: Ford Key Fob Vulnerability Replay Attack
text.text: Weathered Security research found that wireless key fobs of multiple Ford models had vulnerabilities, allowing car doors to be unlocked and engines started using a $300 software-defined radio device. Affected models included the 2017 Ford Expedition, 2019 Ford F-150 Raptor, and 2019 Ford Mustang. The attacker used a software-defined radio to capture the rolling code signal emitted when key fob 1 unlocked the vehicle, then replayed the captured signal, and when key fob 2 was used to unlock, replayed the previously captured signal again. After this process, key fob 1 became inoperable and required a reset to function. During this period, the attacker could replay the signal previously sent by key fob 1 to control the vehicle.

media.caption: Cracking my windshield and earning $10,000 on the Tesla Bug Bounty Program

text.headline: $10,000 XSS Vulnerability on Tesla
text.text: White hat hacker Sam Curry discovered a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in Tesla vehicles that could be used to unauthorizedly obtain vehicle information, such as the vehicle's VIN, speed, temperature, lock status, tire pressure, alarm status, timezone, and other information. Curry exploited this vulnerability on his own Tesla vehicle using an XSS Hunter payload, testing XSS in the vehicle name field (setting a nickname for his car), and ultimately a service technician triggered this stored XSS.

media.caption: Honda Motor Company leaks database with 134 million rows of employee computer data

text.headline: Honda Leaks 40GB Internal Data Due to Database Misconfiguration
text.text: Honda Motors misconfigured an ElasticSearch database containing approximately 134 million files, totaling about 40GB of data. This included data related to Honda's global employee computer networks, such as employee names, employee numbers, departments, employee email addresses, host names, account names, IP addresses, MAC addresses, host names, operating system types, operating system versions, last login times, patch information, and endpoint security status.

media.caption: TESLA MODEL 3 SPOOFED OFF THE HIGHWAY – REGULUS NAVIGATION SYSTEM HACK CAUSES CAR TO TURN ON ITS OWN

text.headline: TESLA MODEL 3 GPS Spoofing
text.text: Regulus Cyber tests showed that using off-the-shelf tools, one could gain control of Tesla's GPS in less than one minute. This spoofing attack caused extreme deceleration and acceleration, rapid lane change suggestions, unnecessary turn signals, multiple attempts to exit the highway at incorrect locations, and extreme driving instability. Relying solely on GPS signals for vehicle self-positioning carries a significant risk of deviation, requiring additional data for correction, such as combined navigation technologies based on visual sensors, RTK/IMU, and other systems.

media.caption: Mercedes-Benz app glitch exposed car owners’ information to other users

text.headline: Mercedes-Benz App Security Vulnerability in US Exposes Other Owners' Information
text.text: The Mercedes-Benz application in the United States had a serious security vulnerability that exposed other owners' personal information. According to tech media TechCrunch, Mercedes-Benz owners in the United States reported that the application (APP) they used to unlock and start their vehicles incorrectly displayed other owners' account and vehicle information, including names, recent activity, phone numbers, and more.

media.caption: Have a Tesla Model 3? This app can track its location

text.headline: Tesla iBeacon Privacy Leak
text.text:
Bluetooth security expert Martin Herfurt's research found that Tesla Model 3 continuously broadcasts a special set of ID numbers (iBeacon) via Bluetooth channels. Tesla uses this set of ID numbers as an important parameter for the mobile APP to open and close doors. However, users had no permission to change or disable this special set of ID numbers, creating an opportunity for malicious actors. By scanning and capturing this set of ID numbers, one could track Tesla Model 3 owners, thereby compromising the personal privacy of vehicle owners. Martin also specifically wrote an APP (Tesla Radar) and built a global Tesla monitoring platform.

iBeacon was originally developed by Apple as a precise micro-location technology using Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). This technology was originally designed to enable merchants to interact more conveniently with customers. However, the designers of iBeacon seemingly did not give much consideration to security and privacy issues. Its characteristic of broadcasting in plaintext via Bluetooth allows anyone to capture and forge its data using a mobile phone or Bluetooth device.

media.caption: Exploiting MARVELL Wireless Protocol Stack Vulnerabilities on TESLA MODEL S

text.headline: Exploiting MARVELL Wireless Protocol Stack Vulnerabilities on TESLA MODEL S
text.text: Tencent Keen Lab researched the wireless function module (the Parrot module with Marvell 88W8688 chip on Model S) and found two vulnerabilities in it. CVE-2019-13581 existed in the wireless chip firmware, and CVE-2019-13582 existed in the wireless chip driver. By combining these two vulnerabilities, an attacker could execute arbitrary commands on the Linux system within the Parrot module.

media.caption: Model Hacking ADAS to Pave Safer Roads for Autonomous Vehicles

text.headline: Adversarial Machine Learning Attack on Tesla and Mobileye ADAS
text.text: The machine learning used in Tesla's assisted driving system had flaws — changes in the physical world could cause these automated assisted driving features to become confused. McAfee researchers used adversarial machine learning to manipulate the Mobileye EyeQ 3 system installed on Tesla vehicles. In the study, a 2-inch piece of electrical tape was used to extend the short horizontal bar in the middle of the number "3" on a "35 mph" speed limit sign. This subtle extension was sufficient to fool the Mobileye EyeQ 3 system into interpreting the 35 mph speed limit as 85 mph, thereby inducing the Tesla vehicle to speed in the speed limit zone.

media.caption: Mercedes-Benz onboard logic unit (OLU) source code leaks online

text.headline: Mercedes-Benz Onboard Logic Unit (OLU) Source Code Leaked
text.text: Daimler failed to properly implement the account confirmation process, which allowed a researcher to register an account on the company's official GitLab server using a non-existent Daimler corporate email address. The researcher downloaded 580 Git repositories from the server and made them public. The leaked projects included not only the source code of Mercedes-Benz OLU components, but also source code for Raspberry Pi images, server images, internal Daimler components for managing remote OLUs, internal documentation, code samples, and more.

media.caption: Tesla Model 3 Hack – Disable Entire Tesla Model 3 Interface

text.headline: Tesla Model 3 Infotainment System Denial of Service Vulnerability (CVE-2020-10558)
text.text: Tesla Model 3's Driving Interface versions prior to 2020.4.10 contain a security vulnerability that stems from the program's failure to properly isolate processes. By tricking the vehicle owner into visiting a specially crafted webpage, the Chromium-based infotainment dashboard system interface can be crashed. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to disable the speedometer, web browser, climate control, navigation, autopilot indicators, and other functions.

media.caption: Tencent Keen Lab: Lexus Vehicle Security Research Overview Report

text.headline: Tencent Keen Lab: Lexus Vehicle Security Research Overview Report
text.text: After conducting security research on the 2017 Lexus NX300 model, Keen Lab discovered a series of security issues in the vehicle's Bluetooth and vehicle diagnostic functions, and was able to compromise the security of the AVN system, in-vehicle CAN network, and related Electronic Control Units (ECUs). By combining the exploitation of these security issues, Keen Lab was able to wirelessly compromise and control the vehicle's AVN system without any user interaction, sending malicious CAN commands to the in-vehicle CAN network, thereby executing unintended physical operations on the vulnerable vehicle.

media.caption: Critical traffic light system vulnerability could cause ‘chaos’ on the roads

text.headline: CVE-2020-12493: Critical Vulnerability in Traffic Signal Systems Enables Manual Manipulation and Traffic Paralysis
text.text:
SWARCO, a leading traffic signal controller manufacturer, was disclosed to have a critical vulnerability. Hackers can exploit this critical vulnerability to disrupt traffic signals, arbitrarily switch traffic lights, and cause traffic paralysis or even traffic accidents.

German industrial cybersecurity consulting firm ProtectEM discovered during a security audit of a German city that SWARCO's CPU LS4000 traffic light controller has a debuggable open port that is susceptible to exploitation by hackers. This vulnerability is an "improper access control" vulnerability that can be exploited by hackers to obtain root access to the device without requiring access authorization.

SWARCO traffic controllers use BlackBerry QNX RTOS, with the QNX debugging application being qconn, and the debug interface is open on port 8000. By exploiting the debug interface, system control can be obtained.

This vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2020-12493 with a CVSS score of 10. It was reported to the vendor in July 2019, and SWARCO provided a patch to customers in April 2020.

media.caption: 360 Sky-Go Team Releases 'Mercedes-Benz Security Research Report': 19 Vulnerabilities Discovered and Patched Collaboratively

text.headline: 360 Sky-Go Team Releases 'Mercedes-Benz Security Research Report': 19 Vulnerabilities Discovered and Patched Collaboratively
text.text: The 360 Sky-Go team conducted an information security testing study on Mercedes-Benz. The subjects of this security research included major connected modules such as the Head-Unit, HERMES (TCU), ATP Protocol, and Backend Services. The research lasted one year and discovered a total of 19 security vulnerabilities. By chaining these vulnerabilities into an attack chain, it was estimated that over 2 million Mercedes-Benz vehicles in China could be affected.

media.caption: Tesla NFC Relay Attack (CVE-2020-15912)

text.headline: Tesla NFC Relay Attack (CVE-2020-15912)
text.text: Kevin 2600 and his team Tiger-Team conducted research and testing on relay attacks against Tesla NFC keys. They successfully implemented a relay attack on the Tesla Model 3's NFC key via Wi-Fi, enabling them to unlock the vehicle doors.

media.caption: KOFFEE - Kia OFFensivE Exploit

text.headline: Kia Fifth-Generation Infotainment System Contains Multiple Vulnerabilities
text.text:
The Kia fifth-generation infotainment system Gen 5.0 is used in over 40 countries worldwide and runs on Android OS version 4.2.2. Versions below 20.06 can access engineering mode through specific methods, enabling the installation of applications from unknown sources via the settings page. Using the built-in browser to download APK files, combined with the enabled application installation, arbitrary application installation can be achieved. After gaining system access, existing programs can be used to send CAN messages to the multimedia CAN bus. Additionally, there are several vulnerabilities whose details have not yet been publicly disclosed, including remote code execution via wireless; writing an APP to invoke system IPC for arbitrary code execution; generating CAN packets and MICON signals based on DBC files, etc.

· CVE-2020-8539: In Kia infotainment system versions SOP.003.30.18.0703, SOP.005.7.181019, and SOP.007.1.191209, an attacker can inject unauthorized commands. Using the micomd program, an attacker can send arbitrary CAN messages to the M-CAN (multimedia CAN) network to set volume, switch songs, control screen brightness, etc. The exploit code for this component, KOFFEE (Kia OFFensivE Exploit), has been integrated into the Metasploit penetration testing framework.

media.caption: X-in-the-Middle : Attacking Fast Charging Piles and Electric Vehicles

text.headline: Frictionless Payment Charging Piles Contain Critical Security Vulnerability with Fraudulent Charging Risk
text.text:
GeekPwn2020 International Security Geek Competition concluded in Shanghai, where the Tencent team Blade Team successfully demonstrated a vulnerability attack on "frictionless payment" DC charging piles. During the competition, Blade Team security researchers simulated an attacker's perspective, requiring only the victim's vehicle identity identifier and a special device to connect the "frictionless payment" DC charging pile with the vehicle. They were able to exploit the charging pile communication protocol vulnerability to easily complete the "fraudulent charging" operation.

Plug-and-charge and frictionless payment are the mainstream development trends in the current charging pile industry. Charging piles using "frictionless payment" technology only require user identity authentication during the initial binding phase. During charging, the vehicle identity is automatically recognized, and after charging is completed, the corresponding amount is deducted from the bound account. The vulnerability discovered this time is a defect at the charging communication protocol level, and all "frictionless payment" DC charging piles using the same technical solution are affected.

media.caption: A code signing bypass for the VW Polo

text.headline: CVE-2020-28656: Volkswagen Polo Local Upgrade Verification Bypass
text.text: The Volkswagen Polo 2019 infotainment system upgrade contains a vulnerability that allows an attacker with physical access to achieve arbitrary code execution. Certain content in the metainfo file within the upgrade package lacks verification, which enables an attacker to write programs to the system and execute them with root privileges.

media.caption: Belgian security researchers from KU Leuven and imec demonstrate serious flaws in Tesla Model X keyless entry system

text.headline: Tesla Model X Bluetooth Key Vulnerability
text.text: Belgian KU Leuven security researcher Lennert Wouters discovered that the Tesla Model X keyless entry system lacks firmware update verification. Hackers can rewrite the key fob firmware via Bluetooth connection, extract the unlock code from the key fob, and then use it to steal a Model X. The entire process can be completed in just a few minutes.

media.caption: Tesla Navigation Crashes on 'Kaiyuan Road Mahi-Mahi Soup' — NTU Professor Finds the Cause
media.credit: How to View Tesla Navigation Voice Input 'Kaiyuan Road Mahi-Mahi Soup' Causing Infotainment Screen Blackout and Crash?

text.headline: Tesla Navigation Voice Input 'Kaiyuan Road Mahi-Mahi Soup' Causes Infotainment Screen Blackout and Crash?
text.text:
In February 2021, it circulated online that the Tesla navigation system would crash upon hearing the phrase "Kaiyuan Road Mahi-Mahi Soup" (seven Chinese characters). Notably, when a location in Tesla navigation contains the rare Chinese character 'tuo' (used in the name for mahi-mahi fish), additional garbled text is displayed.

Hypothesis 1: Tesla crashes because it does not support the Unicode encoding of the character 'tuo'.
Hypothesis 2: 'Kaiyuan Road Mahi-Mahi Soup' (in Chinese) sounds like 'Kindly root to boot again'.

media.caption: TBONE – A zero-click exploit for Tesla MCUs

text.headline: Two White-Hat Hackers Use Drone to 'Hack' Tesla
text.text: Two overseas hackers remotely exploited a zero-click vulnerability via a drone. They successfully compromised the Tesla infotainment system and also opened the vehicle doors and trunk. The attack was carried out by having the Tesla vehicle (e.g., Model 3) automatically connect to the 'Tesla Service' Wi-Fi. Combined with two vulnerabilities in two components of the ConnMan daemon, they achieved remote code execution on the CID (infotainment system): a stack overflow in the DNS forwarder and a stack information leak in the DHCP component.

media.caption: Tencent Keen Lab: Mercedes-Benz Vehicle Information Security Research Overview Report

text.headline: Tencent Keen Lab: Mercedes-Benz Vehicle Information Security Research Overview Report
text.text: After conducting comprehensive and in-depth research on the hardware and software of the latest Mercedes-Benz in-vehicle infotainment system MBUX, Keen Lab discovered multiple related vulnerabilities and successfully exploited them on certain attack surfaces of the Head Unit and T-Box.

media.caption: Canadian software developer discovers Bluetooth key vulnerability that allows anyone to unlock a Tesla, fix deployed through OTA update

text.headline: Canadian Programmer Discovers Bluetooth Key Vulnerability Allowing Anyone to Unlock Tesla
text.text: Canadian programmer Shankar Gomare discovered a Tesla vulnerability while developing Voice for Tesla. This vulnerability can be exploited to unlock any Tesla vehicle. Tesla vehicles are programmed to search for the strongest Bluetooth signal among connected devices within range before deciding to unlock, which is typically the owner's paired mobile device. When this occurs, the vehicle communicates with the Bluetooth device, verifies it is near the vehicle, and sends an unlock code. A coding defect causes BLE connections to not require authentication before connecting to the vehicle. Therefore, by impersonating a phone key, an attacker can force the vehicle to request the unlock code from the actual mobile device when the door handle is pulled, thereby unlocking any Tesla.

media.caption: Volkswagen hack: 3 million customers have had their information stolen

text.headline: Volkswagen 3.3 Million Customer Data Leaked
text.text: The data of 3.3 million Volkswagen Group customers was leaked. The leak occurred because a supplier exposed customer data "unprotected" on the internet between August 2019 and May 2021. Customer information of 3.1 million US Audi customers, 163,000 Canadian Audi customers, and 3,300 US Volkswagen brand customers may have been leaked, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and license plate numbers. Additionally, "more confidential" data of 90,000 US and Canadian customers was leaked, including loan eligibility information and Social Security numbers.

media.caption: Mercedes-Benz USA Announces Initial Findings of Data Investigation Affecting Customers and Interested Buyers

text.headline: Mercedes-Benz Data Breach Affects Nearly 1,000 Users, Including Driver's Licenses and Credit Card Information
text.text: On June 11, 2021, a supplier notified Mercedes-Benz USA (MBUSA) that sensitive personal information of Mercedes-Benz customers and interested buyers had been inadvertently accessible on a cloud storage platform. The data included self-reported credit scores, driver's licenses, Social Security numbers, and credit card information that customers and potential sellers had entered on dealer and company websites between January 2014 and June 2017. Mercedes-Benz evaluated 1.6 million customer records, including customer names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, and some purchased vehicle information, to determine the impact. The data breach exposed the credit card information, Social Security numbers, and driver's license numbers of fewer than 1,000 Mercedes-Benz customers and potential buyers.

media.caption: Schneider Charging Pile Vulnerability Hunting Journey

text.headline: Schneider Charging Pile Vulnerabilities
text.text:
At the end of 2020, security researchers BaCde and Kevin2600 conducted vulnerability hunting on Schneider charging piles, ultimately achieving remote root shell access in a no-user-interaction scenario. Two of the high-severity vulnerabilities are:

CVE-2021-22707: The web backend contains hardcoded credentials. Adding CURLTOKEN=b35fcdc1ea1221e6dd126e172a0131c5a;SESSIONID=admin in the cookie can bypass login authentication and obtain administrator privileges for the web backend service.

CVE-2021-22708: The firmware signature verification algorithm has a defect. A malicious upgrade package carefully crafted by an attacker can bypass verification. By flashing malicious firmware, the root shell of the charging pile can be obtained.

media.caption: Honda Accord, Civic, Acura and Other Models' Wireless Keys Vulnerable to Replay Attacks

text.headline: Honda Accord, Civic, Acura and Other Models Contain Wireless Key Replay Attack Vulnerability
text.text:
Keys for certain Honda Accord, Acura, and Civic models do not use rolling codes but instead employ insecure fixed codes, making the key signals replayable. Attackers can unlock doors, control windows, open the trunk, etc. However, there may be no mitigation, as Honda has ignored CVE-2019-20626.
Confirmed affected models are as follows:
• 2009 Acura TSX
• 2016 Honda Accord V6 Touring Sedan
• 2017 Honda HR-V (CVE-2019-20626)
• 2018 Honda Civic Hatchback
• 2020 Honda Civic LX

media.caption: QNX-2021-001 Vulnerability in the C Runtime Library Impacts BlackBerry QNX Software Development Platform (SDP)

text.headline: QNX Affected by BadAlloc Vulnerability
text.text:
BlackBerry's QNX Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) contains a critical vulnerability (CVE-2021-22156) that could allow malicious actors to compromise and control a variety of products, including automotive, medical devices, and industrial equipment. The vulnerability is an integer overflow in the calloc() function in the C runtime library, affecting QNX Software Development Platform (SDP) 6.5.0SP1 and earlier, QNX OS for Medical 1.1 and earlier, and QNX OS for Safety 1.0.1 and earlier. Successful exploitation could lead to denial of service or arbitrary code execution.

Many automakers including BMW, Audi, and Volkswagen use QNX as their underlying system. Domestic manufacturers such as NIO and XPeng also use this system. Globally, a total of 195 million vehicles use this system, so the disclosure of this vulnerability will affect many vehicle owners.

BadAlloc is the name given by researchers to the discovered memory overflow class of vulnerabilities, as they all originate from the use of vulnerable memory functions such as malloc, calloc, realloc, memalign, valloc, pvalloc, etc. Researchers found that memory allocation implementations in IoT devices and embedded software over the years did not perform adequate input validation. Without input validation, attackers can exploit these memory allocation functions to execute heap overflows, leading to malicious code execution. The Microsoft research team discovered these 25 vulnerabilities, affecting a large number of smart IoT devices and industrial equipment. These vulnerabilities exist in standard memory allocation functions widely used in Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS), embedded Software Development Kits (SDKs), and C standard library (libc) implementations.

media.caption: What Liabilities Might He Face? How Does ETC Work?

text.headline: Man Uses Sunflower Seed Bag to Shield ETC, Evading Tolls 22 Times Over 3 Months Totaling Over 40,000 Yuan
text.text:
A truck driver surnamed Yang from Wuxi, Jiangsu, who frequently traveled between Hangzhou and Beijing, was reported for evading highway tolls. During police interrogation, Yang admitted to using the tin foil from sunflower seed packaging bags to shield ETC and CPC signals. He would cover the ETC device when passing through expensive toll sections and restore it right before exiting the highway. When exiting, the toll station, unable to identify the vehicle's actual travel trajectory, would charge the cheapest toll plan, thereby evading tolls. Statistics showed that Yang evaded tolls 22 times over 3 months, totaling over 40,000 yuan.

ETC Principle: When a vehicle equipped with ETC passes through an ETC lane, the OBU (the small box installed on the windshield) and the RSU (the antenna above the ETC lane) conduct bidirectional communication and data exchange using the Dedicated Short Range Communication (DSRC) protocol. The OBU sends stored vehicle identification information to the RSU, which after receiving and processing the data, automatically identifies the vehicle, performs billing and deduction, and sends a signal to the mechanical barrier to raise and allow passage.

media.caption: Notice of cyber security breach by third party

text.headline: Volvo Cars Discloses Security Breach Leading to R&D Data Theft
text.text:
On December 10, Volvo stated in its announcement that "Volvo Cars has become aware that one of its file repositories has been illegally accessed by a third party." This incident caused its Stockholm stock to drop 3.5% to 72.44 kronor (8.00 USD, 7.06 EUR).

The Snatch ransomware gang has claimed responsibility for this attack. The ransomware group added an entry on its data leak site on November 30, detailing the breach of Volvo Car Corporation's servers and theft of files, accompanied by screenshots of the stolen files as evidence.

media.caption: Radio station snafu in Seattle bricks some Mazda infotainment systems

text.headline: Seattle Mazda Infotainment Systems Bricked by Radio Signal
text.text:
According to the Seattle Times, Mazda models from 2014 to 2017 in Seattle experienced infotainment system crashes and infinite reboots (bricking) after tuning into KUOW 94.9 FM on January 30. After contacting the local Mazda dealer for inspection, they stated that the "connectivity master unit" was damaged and needed replacement.

Cause of the issue: Mazda responded that the radio station sent an image file without a file extension in the HD Radio stream. The infotainment system identifies files based on the file extension (rather than the file header). Due to the absence of a file extension, an exception was triggered, causing the infotainment system to brick.

media.caption: Toyota halts operations at all Japan plants due to cyberattack

text.headline: Supplier Suffers Cyberattack, Toyota Announces One-Day Halt at All Japan Plants
text.text:
On February 28, Toyota supplier Kojima Press Industry reported experiencing a cybersecurity attack. The company primarily supplies plastic parts and electronic components to automakers.

This incident also caused all of Toyota's domestic plants in Japan to halt production for one day on March 1. According to Toyota's statement, production lines at its 14 plants nationwide in Japan resumed on March 2. The March 1 shutdown affected the production of approximately 13,000 vehicles.

According to Kojima Press Industry, it discovered an error on a file server on Saturday evening (February 26). In another statement, the company said that after restarting the server, it confirmed a virus infection and discovered a threatening message.

A single supplier being hacked was enough to halt production at Toyota, one of the world's largest automakers, for a day, raising concerns about the vulnerability of Japanese companies' supply chains. Critics of the Japanese government stated that cybersecurity has become a key area of concern for Japan, and that a hack on a previously obscure supplier was sufficient to bring Toyota, one of the world's most powerful manufacturers, to a standstill domestically.

text.headline: Tire Giant Bridgestone Hit by Ransomware Attack, Factory Production Halted
text.text:
On February 27, employees at Bridgestone Americas (BSA)'s La Vergne, Tennessee factory reported a temporary shutdown due to a cybersecurity incident. The company immediately launched an investigation and engaged consulting firm Accenture Security to assess the incident's impact. To prevent potential spread, the company disconnected network connections at multiple manufacturing and retreading facilities in Latin America and North America. The company's statement noted that the investigation is still ongoing, and the specific scope or nature of the incident cannot yet be determined, but the company will continue its efforts to protect the safety of operations, data, employees, and customers.

As a result of the attack, the factory was shut down for over ten days before fully resuming production on March 10. The company is working closely with Accenture Security to analyze the details of the incident and confirm the types of data stolen. Bridgestone emphasized that the security of employee, customer, and partner information remains a top priority.

Following the incident, Bridgestone proactively notified US federal law enforcement agencies and maintained ongoing communication. Bridgestone stated that it will continue to take measures to strengthen cybersecurity and prevent similar incidents from recurring.

media.caption: Notice of Unauthorized Access to Group Company

text.headline: DENSO German Subsidiary Hit by Cyberattack, 1.4TB of Data Stolen
text.text:
On March 14, DENSO stated in its announcement that on March 10 local time, it detected unauthorized malware access at its German subsidiary responsible for sales and engineering. Spokesperson Izumi Saito stated that DENSO responded quickly and that the company's business operations were not affected by the attack.

Japanese cybersecurity firm Mitsui Bussan Secure Directions reported that a group named Pandora threatened to disclose DENSO's trade secrets on the dark web, including business emails, invoices, and parts drawings. The group claimed to have obtained over 157,000 purchase orders, emails, and drawings, with a total data size of approximately 1.4TB. Pandora launched the cyberattack using ransomware, which encrypts company data. Companies that do not want their data leaked must pay a ransom to the hackers.

This incident marks the second cyberattack on a Toyota supplier in recent times. Two weeks earlier (March 1), Toyota temporarily closed all of its plants in Japan due to an attack on the systems of its supplier Kojima Press Industry.

media.caption: Grand Theft Auto — Playing with Rolling Codes (Part 2)

text.headline: Honda Car Key Rolling Code Design Flaw, Wireless Signals Can Be Replayed (CVE-2021-46145)
text.text:
Qianxin Xingyu Lab researcher Kevin2600 discovered a design flaw in Honda car keys. Based on the design principles of rolling codes, simple replay attacks typically cannot unlock car doors. However, if expired unlock commands are rearranged in a specific order and retransmitted, surprisingly, the Honda vehicle's synchronization counter rolls back, meaning that previously expired unlock commands become valid again.

As early as 2016, a researcher had found the same type of issue in BYD car key design.

media.caption: Tesla-Charging-Port-Opener

text.headline: Tesla Charging Port Cover Replay Vulnerability (CVE-2022-27948)
text.text:
The charging head of Tesla Supercharger stations is equipped with a button for opening the charging port cover. This button unlocks the charging port cover by sending a wireless radio frequency signal. Since the wireless signal used for unlocking employs a fixed code, an attacker can replay a previously recorded wireless signal to open the charging port cover at any location. This vulnerability was discovered and exploited years ago, and dedicated wireless keys for unlocking the charging port cover are even available for sale.

It is worth noting that the frequency of the wireless radio frequency signal differs between domestic and international markets. The frequency used internationally is 315MHz, while the frequency used domestically (in China) is 433MHz.

media.caption: PoC for vulnerability in Honda's Remote Keyless System(CVE-2022-27254)

text.headline: Honda Keyless Entry System Replay Attack (CVE-2022-27254)
text.text:
CBlake Berry and Ayyappan Rajesh discovered that the wireless keys of certain Honda and Acura vehicles not only fail to use rolling codes but also lack encryption. A hacker in proximity to the vehicle can exploit the keyless entry system vulnerability to unlock doors and remotely start the engine. This vulnerability can be used for replay attacks, where the attacker eavesdrops on the RF signals sent by the wireless key to the vehicle. After capturing these signals, retransmitting them enables arbitrary unlocking of the vehicle.

Affected models: 2016-2020 Honda Civic (LX, EX, EX-L, Touring, Si, Type R)

media.caption: Charging Pile Vulnerability Hunting Practice

text.headline: Xingyu Lab Discloses Vulnerabilities in Multiple Charging Pile Models
text.text:
Xingyu Lab security researchers discovered that many charging piles have independent IP addresses and are exposed to the public internet. Through research on the EBEE CC charging controller and GARO Wallbox, the security of charging piles was found to be relatively weak. The vulnerabilities discovered during this research are as follows.

The EBEE CC series charging controller is a core component of charging piles from companies such as GARO, ENSTO, and Bender. The charging controller is the brain of the charging pile, responsible for upper-layer communication to connect remotely to cloud services for remote control, and at the lower end, it connects to electrical equipment to manage charging between the pile and the vehicle.
· CVE-2021-34601: SSH hardcoded credentials were found in the firmware, but the user's permissions are at a normal level. Privilege escalation can be achieved using CVE-2021-34602.
· CVE-2021-34602: Using the CVE-2021-34601 hardcoded credentials, after entering the system, plaintext-stored web backend account credentials and passwords were discovered. Normal users can also view these. After logging in, a command injection vulnerability was found.

The Wi-Fi module (which also serves as the main TCU) used in the GARO Wallbox GLB/GTB/GTC is based on Raspberry Pi development. The charging pile web backend does not even have any identity protection mechanism enabled, and additionally contains command injection vulnerabilities. It is particularly noteworthy that unauthorized users can call the API /freecharge interface to achieve free charging.
· CVE-2021-45876: The web backend lacks access control, allowing anyone to view and modify charging pile configurations.
· CVE-2021-45877: The web middleware Tomcat Manager uses hardcoded credentials.
· CVE-2021-45878: Unauthorized command injection, the url parameter of the firmware update downloadAndUpdate module contains a command injection vulnerability.

media.caption: Tesla BLE Phone-as-a-Key Passive Entry Vulnerable to Relay Attacks

text.headline: Tesla Model 3/Y Bluetooth Link Layer Relay Attack
text.text:
NCC disclosed a vulnerability in the keyless entry system of Tesla Model 3 and Model Y. By relaying Bluetooth link layer data from the keyless entry system, the vehicle can be unlocked and started. In the research, several researchers used two specially programmed small relay devices with a total cost of less than 100 USD. One relay device A was placed within approximately 14 meters of the Tesla owner's smartphone or key fob (capable of sniffing and capturing the key signal); the other relay device B was connected to a laptop and brought near the vehicle. Through communication between the two devices, the key signal captured by device A was forwarded and amplified, allowing the vehicle to recognize the signal. In this way, even if the smart key is not within the vehicle's originally designed communication range, the vehicle would still receive the key's signal and then unlock and start. Once communication was established, the entire hacking process could be completed in just 10 seconds.

Device manufacturers generally employ two methods to defend against relay attacks. One defensive measure is to measure the latency of request and response traffic and reject authentication when the delay reaches a specific threshold, since relay communication typically takes longer to complete than legitimate communication. Another protective measure is to encrypt the credentials sent by the phone.

Unlike previous BLE relay attacks, the key to the successful bypass is that it captures data from the baseband, where wireless signals are sent to and received from devices, and captures data at the link layer (the lowest layer of the Bluetooth protocol stack), where connections are advertised, created, maintained, and terminated. Previous BLE relay attacks operated at the GATT (Generic Attribute Profile) layer, which is at a higher level in the stack. The researchers directly bypassed the credential encryption process through link layer relay, i.e., bypassing the second defensive measure employed by device manufacturers. This relay method is not limited to Tesla but also applies to other IoT devices using BLE.

media.caption: Hardwear.io
media.credit: Opening Doors and Stealing Cars: Bluetooth LE Link Layer Relay Attacks

text.headline: BLE Link Layer Relay Attack
text.text:
BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) link layer relay attack: By forwarding data at the link layer from the baseband, known relay attack protections can be bypassed — including link layer encryption and GATT latency bounding. This enables long-distance compromise of BLE-based proximity authentication, affecting devices such as vehicles, smart door locks, building security systems, mobile devices, and laptops that use BLE technology for authentication.

At Hardwear.io, NCC Principal Security Consultant SULTAN QASIM KHAN shared details of Sniffle Relay, the world's first Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) link layer relay attack. Sniffle is an open-source BLE communication sniffing tool developed by NCC, and the relay tool designed based on it has not been publicly released. Previously, SULTAN QASIM KHAN had already used this tool to unlock and start a Tesla Model 3/Y (see the event 'Tesla Model 3/Y Bluetooth Link Layer Relay Attack').

media.caption: Project TEMPA

text.headline: Arbitrary Creation of Tesla Bluetooth Keys
text.text:
Martin Herfurt from Trifinite discovered a method to register new keys for Tesla vehicles. Within 130 seconds of unlocking with an NFC key, an attacker can communicate with the vehicle body BLE Bluetooth key module and register a new key. Exploiting this flaw in the key system allows the creation of brand-new Bluetooth keys.


Additionally, they found that sending specific BLE messages can bypass PIN2DRIVE.

media.caption: Found a Few Keys on Google and Cracked a Hyundai Car?

text.headline: Hyundai/Kia Local Update Cracked
text.text:
From May to June 2022, software engineer Daniel Feldman published four blog posts documenting his process and methods for cracking his Hyundai vehicle's infotainment system. The most critical step was obtaining the private key that Hyundai uses to manage software. This was supposed to be impossible, but on a whim he searched on Google and actually found the private key, then successfully cracked his own car. Hyundai Mobis made some elementary mistakes in creating local update packages — using an AES encryption example key as the official key. This would allow anyone to repackage update packages, embed malicious programs, and successfully write them into the infotainment system. The two major issues are as follows.

1. Hyundai encrypted the local update packages. However, Feldman discovered a special update program on Hyundai's update website. After downloading it, he found that a set of files matched a program name inside the firmware archive. By using a ZIP decompression tool to verify file CRCs, he found bkcrack plaintext in a pair of matching files. After a series of decryption and programming operations, he ultimately succeeded in extracting all files from the encrypted firmware ZIP archive and began reverse engineering.

2. While analyzing the firmware update files, Feldman found a large number of files with the "enc_" prefix, all of which were encrypted. Without being able to read these files, it would be impossible to understand the system's update process. From the open-source code downloaded from the Mobis website, he discovered the linux_envsetup.sh file, which is a script used to create system update ZIP files. The ZIP password required for system updates, encryption method, AES symmetric cipher block chaining (CBC) encryption key, and the IV (initialization vector) value used to encrypt firmware images were all in the script. The AES key and IV were the first AES 128-bit CBC example keys listed in the NIST-published SP800-38A document, but Hyundai's developers directly used the keys from a public document as the encryption keys for their own product's confidential information.

media.caption: Rolling Pwn Attack
media.credit: Hackers can unlock Honda cars remotely in Rolling-PWN attacks

text.headline: Rolling Pwn: RF Key Rolling Code Rollback Vulnerability
text.text:
Kevin2600 and Wesley Li from the Xingyu Lab (StarLab) discovered a design flaw in the rolling code of vehicle radio frequency (RF) keys. Sending consecutive vehicle control commands causes the rolling code counter to roll back, restoring previously used control commands that should have been invalidated. This vulnerability is similar to CVE-2021-46145, previously discovered by the same team. Exploiting this rolling code flaw enables opening vehicle doors and even starting the engine. The newly discovered vulnerability affects multiple vehicle brands, particularly a large number of Honda vehicles from the 2012 model year to the present. The confirmed affected models are as follows.

· Honda Civic 2012
· Honda X-RV 2018
· Honda C-RV 2020
· Honda Accord 2020
· Honda Odyssey 2020
· Honda Inspire 2021
· Honda Fit 2022
· Honda Civic 2022
· Honda VE-1 2022
· Honda Breeze 2022

media.caption: BitSight Discovers Critical Vulnerabilities in Widely Used Vehicle GPS Tracker
media.credit: The full report with technical analysis

text.headline: MiCODUS Vehicle Tracker Security Vulnerabilities Affect Over One Million Vehicles Worldwide
text.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), together with BitSight, published an advisory warning of multiple security vulnerabilities in the MiCODUS MV720 Global Positioning System (GPS) tracker used in over 1.5 million vehicles. BitSight's research identified six vulnerabilities in the MiCODUS (Shenzhen) MV720 GPS vehicle tracker. Attackers could exploit these security vulnerabilities to track any vehicle in real time, access historical routes, and even cut off the engine of a moving vehicle. MiCODUS has 1.5 million devices across 420,000 customers in 169 countries worldwide, with a wide range of applications including private vehicles, law enforcement agencies, military and government customers, and a nuclear power plant operator.

· CVE-2022-2107: The Android application contains a hardcoded credential (7DU2DJFDR8321). Using this hardcoded key allows login to the API server, impersonating users and sending SMS commands to the GPS tracker. This enables remote attackers to send commands directly to the MV720 tracker and gain full control over location information, routes, and geofences. Hackers can track locations in real time, cut off vehicle fuel, and disable car alarms.
· CVE-2022-2141: The API server/GPS tracker has improper authentication, allowing users to send SMS commands directly to the GPS tracker without a password, enabling attackers to "gain a man-in-the-middle position, control all traffic between the GPS tracker and the original server, and gain control of the GPS tracker."
· CVE-2022-2199: A cross-site scripting vulnerability allows attackers to gain control of the GPS tracker by tricking users into making requests.
· CVE-2022-34150: The web server has an authenticated Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability on the parameter "Device ID." This vulnerability allows accepting arbitrary device IDs to access data from the server (https://www.micodus.net/ProductUpdate.aspx?id=XXXX&deviceid=XXXXX&randon=11111) without further verifying the association between the device ID and the user.
· CVE-2022-33944: The MiCODUS web backend (https://www.micodus.net/Report/StopDetail.aspx?id=YYYY&deviceid=XXXXX&randon=1111) has an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability, allowing unauthenticated users to obtain Excel reports of other GPS trackers' activities by specifying the HTTP POST parameter hidDeviceId, including the GPS address and time of vehicle stops.
· All devices have the SMS command configured with the default password 123456, with no enforced policy to change the password. A large number of devices still use the default password.

media.caption: Multiple Shanghai Car Owners Alerted to "Gunfight on the Road"? Police: No Such Incident Occurred

text.headline: Shanghai Car In-Vehicle Displays Show "Gunfight on the Road" Alert?
text.text:
On the 23rd, many Porsche and Audi owners in Shanghai encountered a traffic warning message displaying "Gunfight on the road" on their in-vehicle screens. CCTV reporters verified with the Shanghai Municipal Public Security Bureau and confirmed that no gunfight incident had occurred in Shanghai. Regarding the erroneous vehicle navigation alert, some industry insiders believed it might be a translation issue, while not ruling out the possibility of a hacker attack. To date, no official investigation results have been released. The following are some mainstream speculations.

1. RDS message spoofing: RDS (Radio Data System) can be used for intelligent traffic information distribution systems, broadcasting road traffic information via urban RDS radio stations, and receiving text and icon information through fixed LED screens distributed throughout the city and in-vehicle mobile receivers, enabling traffic guidance, flow management, and other functions. In emergencies, the receiver can be automatically turned on to issue voice or text warnings at a preset volume. Hackers exploited RDS wireless FM radio broadcasting to disseminate the fake message "Gunfight on the road."
2. The message push service was attacked by hackers. The attackers constructed the message "Gunfight on the road" and pushed it to the relevant vehicle models.
3. Since the "Gunfight on the road" alert only appeared on foreign-brand vehicles, a small number of people believed it was a machine translation error that caused the ambiguity.

text.headline: Connected Vehicle Service Provider Sirius XM API Vulnerability: Unauthorized Remote Control of Honda, Nissan, Infiniti, and Acura Vehicles
text.text:
The connected vehicle service provider Sirius XM's remote vehicle control service has an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) vulnerability that allows querying a vehicle's remote control Token using only the VIN. This Token can be used to unlock the vehicle, start the vehicle, and obtain the owner's personal information. The affected vehicles this time were Honda, Nissan, Infiniti, and Acura.

Sirius XM uses HTTP2 to obtain remote service Tokens via the mobile.telematics.net/ha/exchangeToken interface. Security researcher Sam Curry discovered during testing of the POST parameters {"customerId : "nissancust: 129383573" , "vin" :"SFNRL6H82NB044273"} that modifying the POST request content to {"customerId" : "vin: 5FNRL6H82NBe44273"} would retrieve the Token for 5FNRL6H82NBe44273. After obtaining the Token, not only could the owner's personal privacy data be accessed, but the vehicle could also be controlled through other API interfaces, such as remote unlocking, starting, positioning, flashing lights, and honking. More seriously, after modifying the VIN to that of Honda, Nissan, Infiniti, or Acura vehicles that also use Sirius XM services, the Token could still be obtained. This means that unauthorized users could control Honda, Nissan, Infiniti, and Acura vehicles using Sirius XM services.

media.caption: A vulnerability affecting Hyundai and Genesis vehicles

text.headline: Hyundai, Genesis Vehicle Account Takeover
text.text:
The email used during user registration for Hyundai and Genesis has a truncation vulnerability, allowing authorized users to perform remote unlocking, engine start, and other vehicle control operations on other vehicles.

Security researcher Sam Curry discovered that remote vehicle control sends POST data with Access_token:JWT to api.telematics.hyundaiusa.com/ac/v2/rcs/rdo/unlock with {"userName":"EMAIL","vin":"VIN"}, using E-MAIL and Access_token as authentication parameters. In further testing, it was found that user registration did not verify the validity of the email. During fuzzing of the E-MAIL in the userName field, it was discovered that using CRLF could truncate the E-MAIL, tricking the backend service into interpreting victim@gmail.com%0d as victim@gmail.com, achieving account takeover of victim@gmail.com.

media.caption: Weil der Bus-Vorrang an Ampeln in Deutschland noch mit Analogfunk funktionieren, lassen sie durch Dritte fernsteuern.

text.headline: Replay Attack: German Traffic Signals Vulnerable to Manipulation
text.text:
Security researchers demonstrated to journalists from BR, NDR, and c't that they could easily manipulate traffic light systems. Not all intersection traffic signals could be switched to green or red, but traffic signal timing could be artificially extended, which could cause traffic congestion or chaos. To expedite public transit, buses and trams in many German cities have priority. When a vehicle arrives, the traffic light switches to green. The traffic light switching is controlled using unencrypted radio signals at approximately 150.890KHz, and anyone with knowledge of radio technology can control these traffic signals. Replay attacks can easily achieve control over traffic lights.

Traffic lights use centralized and decentralized control. The centralized approach provides a control center that maintains connections with each traffic signal. Priority vehicles do not directly affect the traffic signals; instead, they report to the control center, which forwards the request to the traffic signals. Currently, decentralized control is primarily used, where priority vehicles directly control the corresponding traffic signals. According to Munich's transport authority, the risk was considered low. No city confirmed that the signal had been deliberately exploited.

Experts reminded that decentralized traffic light control should use more modern digital radio standards, such as TETRA or TETRAPOL, rather than insecure analog radio.
