text.headline: Auto Dealer Eagers Automotive Hit by Cyberattack, Forced to Halt Stock Exchange Trading to Assess Impact
text.text:
Eagers Automotive, a leading automotive dealer group in Australia and New Zealand, announced a trading halt on the stock exchange due to a recent cyberattack. The company operates over 300 retail stores for well-known brands including Toyota, BMW, Nissan, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Ford, Volkswagen, and Honda, and owns multiple subsidiaries specializing in used car sales.

The cyberattack caused disruptions to certain information systems in Australia and New Zealand, preventing the completion of sales for some vehicles scheduled for delivery and affecting some service and parts operations. In a subsequent statement, the company confirmed that multiple systems across Australia and New Zealand were impacted by the cyber incident. The disruption to information systems affected the company's operations in the Australian and New Zealand regions. An unauthorized third party accessed parts of the company's information systems, illegally obtaining and deleting some data. The company was sending notifications to a small number of individuals facing serious threats from potential data misuse.

External experts were engaged and launched an urgent investigation. Eagers Automotive notified the Australian Cyber Security Centre and the New Zealand National Cyber Security Centre about the incident.

media.caption: Netgear, Hyundai latest X accounts hacked to push crypto drainers

text.headline: Hyundai MEA's X Account Hijacked to Promote Crypto Drainers
text.text:
The X (Twitter) account of Hyundai MEA (Middle East & Africa) was hijacked. The account name was changed to "Overworld," and multiple tweets were posted to drive traffic to cryptocurrency websites, luring users to register on malicious cryptocurrency sites with attractive offers. When users connected their crypto wallets, the virtual currencies and NFTs in the wallets would be stolen.

Overworld is a cross-platform multiplayer RPG game backed by Binance Labs, the venture capital and incubator division of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Possibly because Overworld is frequently impersonated in similar scams, Overworld often warns its Twitter followers: "Please exercise caution and stay away from those impersonating our account. Only click on links from the official @OverworldPlay Twitter account."

Hyundai has since regained control of the account and removed all links posted by the attackers that redirected users to malicious websites.

Hackers are increasingly targeting verified government and corporate X accounts to lend legitimacy to their malicious tweets, pushing cryptocurrency scams, phishing websites, and crypto drainer sites. During the same period, the X accounts of Netgear and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission were also compromised.

media.caption: Hyundai Motor India fixes bug that exposed customers’ personal data

text.headline: Hyundai Motor India Service Station File Sharing Links Leak Customer Personal Information
text.text:
Hyundai Motor India's subsidiary fixed a vulnerability that affected the personal information of South Asian customers. The leaked information included names, mailing addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, license plate numbers, engine numbers, and mileage. Affected users were those who had their vehicles serviced at authorized service centers in India. TechCrunch (a technology media outlet owned by Yahoo) learned from an anonymous security researcher that the vulnerability was caused by Hyundai Motor India's authorized service centers sharing repair order and invoice retrieval links with customers via WhatsApp during servicing. The links contained phone numbers, which exposed customers' personal information. By changing the phone number in the link, other customers' information could be exposed.

After verifying the researcher's findings, TechCrunch emailed Hyundai Motor India on December 29. Upon receiving a response on January 4, TechCrunch disclosed the vulnerability details to Hyundai Motor India. Due to the simplicity but severity of the vulnerability, TechCrunch requested that Hyundai Motor India fix it within 7 days. On January 11, the vulnerability was fixed, and the relevant links were redirected to an error page and are no longer accessible.

media.caption: PWN2OWN AUTOMOTIVE 2024 - DAY THREE RESULTS
media.credit: REVEALING THE TARGETS AND RULES FOR THE FIRST PWN2OWN AUTOMOTIVE

text.headline: First PWN2OWN Automotive Concludes, 49 Zero-Days Disclosed
text.text:
The first Pwn2Own Automotive competition, held over three days (January 24-26, 2024), concluded with a total of $1,323,750 in bounties awarded, as participants discovered 49 unique zero-day vulnerabilities. Team Synacktiv claimed the Master of Pwn title with $450,000 in bounties and 50 points.

On August 29, 2023, ZDI announced the targets for the first PWN2OWN Automotive, including EV charging stations and in-vehicle operating systems.
- Vehicles: Tesla
- Head units: Sony XAV-AX550, Alpine Halo iLX-F509, Pioneer DMH-WT600NEX
- Charging stations: ChargePoint, Phoenix, EMPORIA, JuiceBOX, Autel, Ubiquiti
- In-vehicle operating systems: AGL, QNX, Android Automotive OS

With the exception of QNX and Android Automotive OS, which no team challenged, Tesla, all charging stations, and the AGL operating system were successfully compromised.

media.caption: Cyber-Attack hits KCATA. Communications affected.

text.headline: Kansas City Area Transportation Authority Hit by Ransomware Attack
text.text:
The Kansas City Area Transportation Authority (KCATA), the primary public transit operator in Kansas City, Missouri, USA, suffered a ransomware attack. KCATA operates subway and 78 bus routes across seven counties in Missouri and Kansas. As of 2022, the company's total ridership exceeded 10.5 million. The day after the attack, KCATA issued a statement announcing that it had launched an investigation with the involvement of external experts and notified relevant authorities, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). The company stated that the cyberattack did not affect transit services, including bus routes and paratransit services. However, it caused disruptions to the regional call center's operations.

The Medusa hacker group claimed responsibility for the attack. On its Tor website, the group posted data samples stolen from KCATA as proof of the attack. The group threatened to publish all stolen data unless KCATA paid a $2 million ransom.

media.caption: How a mistakenly published password exposed Mercedes-Benz source code
media.credit: Mercedes-Benz Source Code at Risk: GitHub Token Mishap Sparks Major Security Concerns

text.headline: Employee Accidentally Leaks Repository Credentials, Mercedes-Benz Source Code at Risk for 4 Months
text.text:
RedHunt Labs' attack surface management research team discovered during routine internet scanning that a Mercedes-Benz employee's authentication token was exposed in a public GitHub repository. The leaked token provided unrestricted access to Mercedes-Benz's internal GitHub Enterprise Server, allowing anyone to retrieve private source code repositories. These included source code, database access credentials, cloud service access credentials, design documents, and more. The token had been exposed online for approximately 4 months since late September 2023. It remains unclear whether any unauthorized parties accessed the internal data. Mercedes-Benz declined to disclose whether any third party had accessed the exposed data.

RedHunt Labs shared its findings with TechCrunch, and with the media's assistance, informed the automaker. TechCrunch disclosed the security issue to Mercedes-Benz on Monday. On Wednesday, Mercedes-Benz spokesperson Katja Liesenfeld confirmed the issue, and the corresponding API token was immediately revoked and the public repository was removed.

media.caption: Hyundai Motor Europe hit by Black Basta ransomware attack

text.headline: Hyundai Motor Europe Hit by Black Basta Ransomware Attack
text.text:
Hyundai Motor Europe, headquartered in Germany, suffered a Black Basta ransomware attack, with 3TB of corporate data stolen.

In early January, upon learning of the attack, security media outlet BleepingComputer contacted Hyundai and was told the company was experiencing IT issues and was working to resolve them as quickly as possible. After further information was shared, Hyundai confirmed that its European division had suffered a cyberattack, with an unauthorized third party accessing restricted networks and stealing 3TB of corporate data.

Black Basta is a ransomware and a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) criminal enterprise that first emerged in early 2022, immediately becoming one of the world's most active RaaS threat actors. Within just the first few months of its operations, it claimed 19 high-profile corporate victims and over 100 confirmed victims. Black Basta conducts highly targeted attacks against organizations in the United States, Japan, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand, rather than employing random attack methods. The group employs a double extortion strategy, encrypting victims' critical data and important servers while threatening to publish sensitive data on its public leak site. It is believed that core members of Black Basta come from the disbanded Conti threat actor group, given similarities in malware development, leak sites, and communication regarding negotiation, payment, and data recovery.

media.caption: VARTA affected by cyber attack
media.credit: VARTA makes good progress in solving the cyberattack

text.headline: German Battery Manufacturer VARTA AG Hit by Cyberattack, Forcing Production Halt
text.text:
VARTA, a subsidiary of Clarios (formerly Johnson Controls Power Solutions), was founded in 1887 in Hagen, Germany, and is one of Europe's most well-known automotive battery brands.

Due to the attack on parts of its IT infrastructure, the company had to shut down its IT systems and disconnect from the internet to ensure security. The overall extent of the damage caused by the incident remains unclear.

In response to the attack, VARTA activated its emergency plan and established a task force composed of cybersecurity experts and computer forensics specialists to assist with system recovery. VARTA's top priority was to ensure data integrity, leading to the decision to proactively shut down systems.

Following the announcement of the cyberattack, production operations at five facilities (Ellwangen, Nordlingen, Dischingen, Brasov/Romania and Batam/Indonesia) were shut down, with no clear timeline for resuming normal operations, causing VARTA's share price to drop 4.75%.

media.caption: Sensitive Information Belonging to BMW Exposed Due to Misconfigured Cloud Bucket

text.headline: BMW Exposes Sensitive Information Due to Misconfigured Cloud Storage Bucket
text.text:
SOCRadar researchers discovered a misconfigured cloud storage bucket exposed by BMW during routine internet public cloud resource scanning. An Azure storage bucket used in the development environment was erroneously configured as publicly accessible. The exposed file (azconfig.io) contained highly sensitive data, such as database connection strings for development and production environments, Azure Docker authentication credentials, and private storage bucket keys. These cloud services affect North America, Europe, and China.

BMW's response to the data breach: the company will strengthen continuous monitoring of cloud resources; the leaked data does not affect customer or personal information.

media.caption: Take a glance of browser, I find Cybellum RCE

text.headline: CVE-2023-42419: Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Cybellum Product Security Platform
text.text:
The Cybellum Product Security Platform is one of the most widely used products for automotive firmware security testing and management. The platform is widely used by OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, and testing organizations, including automakers such as BMW, Audi, Nissan, Great Wall Motors, Jaguar Land Rover, and Hozon Auto; suppliers such as Denso, Harman, Veoneer, Faurecia, and Mobileye; and testing organizations such as CATARC, CAERI, CCID, and CEPREI.

Security researchers @Delikely from the Xingyu Lab and @Imweekend from CAERI discovered a security flaw in the platform: it contained a reserved backdoor interface capable of executing arbitrary code. Although this interface was protected -- only signed and encrypted data could be executed -- the implementation incorrectly used the signing and encryption keys, using the same key set for both signing and encryption/decryption. Furthermore, the keys were stored in plaintext within the platform and could be easily obtained. By using the keys to encrypt and sign an attack payload, arbitrary code execution could be achieved.

The product testing platform in use contained detection records with large amounts of sensitive information, such as unencrypted firmware, private keys, and testing reports. Cybellum has since released an update to fix this vulnerability. Users within their license period are recommended to apply the update, while those with expired licenses are advised to take the platform offline.

media.caption: Nearly 600,000 Records Exposed Online in Leading EV-Service Provider Data Breach

text.headline: Leading North American EV Service Provider Suffers Data Breach, Nearly 600,000 Records Exposed Online
text.text:
Qmerit is a company specializing in EV charging solutions, engaged in the installation and maintenance of EV charging infrastructure, and partners with multiple top-tier automakers. In 2024, Qmerit was selected as the preferred installer for General Motors energy residential products and claims to have completed over 269,000 charger installations across North America.

Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered an unprotected database belonging to EV service provider Qmerit, exposing 573,309 records. The exposed database totaled 585.81 GB and contained a large volume of documents, including invoices, price quotes, electrical permits, and customer-submitted survey information, including details such as images of their homes and charger locations. This breach could lead to identity theft, fraud, and privacy issues.

Qmerit secured the database promptly upon receiving notification. The company also advised customers and contractors to verify suspicious requests and ensure data security.

media.caption: Data Breach Notifications
media.credit: Ransomware attack on Nissan North America results in employee data loss

text.headline: Nissan North America Hit by Attack Resulting in Employee Data Loss
text.text:
Nissan North America (NNA) notified consumers on May 15 that a ransomware attack resulted in the loss of some personal information related to NNA employees, including Social Security numbers. In a filing with the Maine Attorney General's Office, NNA stated that the cybersecurity incident affected 53,038 individuals, including both NNA employees and consumers.

The breach date was November 7, 2023. NNA informed all current employees about the incident at a town hall meeting on December 5, stating that some employees' personal information may have been accessed and that NNA would notify affected individuals following the investigation. NNA stated in the filing that the actual breach was discovered on February 28 of this year. NNA stated that through its investigation, it learned that the criminal threat actor accessed data from multiple local and network shares at NNA, but did not encrypt any data or render any of NNA's systems inoperable.

A Nissan spokesperson stated that the automaker became aware of the attack when a threat actor deliberately accessed and caused a brief shutdown of some non-production systems.

NNA stated that since the attack, it has taken multiple measures to strengthen its security environment, including enterprise-wide password resets, implementing Carbon Black monitoring on all compatible systems, vulnerability scanning, and other measures to address unauthorized access.

media.caption: FORM 8-K REPORT

text.headline: Advance Auto Parts Suffers Massive Data Breach Due to Third-Party Cloud Data Service Attack
text.text:
Advance Auto Parts, a leading automotive parts and accessories retailer, operates 4,777 stores and 320 Worldpac branches in the United States, with branches in Canada, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. It also serves 1,152 independently owned Carquest brand stores in these regions as well as in Mexico and various Caribbean islands.

On a data breach forum, a data seller named Sp1d3r claimed to have stolen 3TB of data from Advance Auto Parts' Snowflake cloud storage. The stolen information was offered for sale at $1.5 million. It included:
· 380 million customer records, including names, emails, mobile phone numbers, phone numbers, addresses, etc.
· 44 million membership card/fuel card numbers and associated customer details.
· Information on 358,000 employees;
· Automotive parts and part numbers;
· 140 million customer orders;
· Sales history data;
· Employment candidate information, including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and demographic details;
· Transaction bid details;
· Over 200 tables of various data types, etc.;

The Advance Auto Parts data breach is part of a series of recent attacks targeting customers of cloud storage company Snowflake. Prior to this incident, Live Nation, the parent company of Ticketmaster, also suffered a major data breach. Hackers claimed to have stolen personal details of 560 million customers, with the stolen data hosted on Snowflake's cloud storage.

In response to the intrusion, Snowflake and third-party cybersecurity experts CrowdStrike and Mandiant issued a joint statement saying they are investigating targeted threat activity against certain Snowflake customer accounts. They are working to understand the extent of the intrusion and mitigate its impact.

media.caption: Securities Exchange
media.credit: US car dealers are feeling the pain of CDK cyberattack

text.headline: Automotive Software Provider CDK Global Extorted for $25 Million
text.text:
CDK Global is a leading global automotive technology solutions provider, offering CRM, dealer management systems (DMS), networking and communication technology products and services for automotive dealers, serving over 15,000 dealer customers worldwide with thousands of employees.

The attack occurred in mid-June, when CDK Global was hit by two consecutive ransomware attacks, forcing its data centers and IT systems to shut down. The impact spread rapidly, affecting dealerships using CDK Global's services including Asbury Automotive Group, AutoNation, Group 1 Automotive, Lithia Motors, and Sonic Automotive. With sales, transaction, and inventory management operations disrupted, most business operations came to a standstill, forcing dealers to process orders with pen and paper, which affected vehicle sales for that month.

CDK Global reportedly paid a $25 million ransom to the ransomware group BlackSuit to restore core systems disrupted by the ransomware attack.

text.headline: Automotive Dealer Modern Auto Hit by BlackByte Ransomware Attack
text.text:
Modern Auto is an automotive dealer in North Carolina, USA, selling new vehicles from brands including Cadillac, Chevrolet, Ford, Hyundai, Mazda, and Toyota, as well as used vehicles.

On July 18, BlackByte publicly released 4.2GB of Modern Auto's data as a sample and demanded a ransom of $65 million.

text.headline: BMW Hong Kong Leaks 14,000 Customer Records
text.text:
In July 2024, approximately 14,000 BMW (Hong Kong) customer records were leaked, with the data posted on an active hacker forum.

BMW Hong Kong stated that the incident involved information processed by a third-party organization handling customer data. The investigation found that 14,000 customer records, including names and mobile phone numbers, were leaked. The company reported the incident to police and notified the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, while also engaging external cybersecurity experts to conduct a comprehensive investigation.

media.caption: Hacking Digital License Plates with Fault Injection
media.credit: Hackers Can Jailbreak Digital License Plates to Make Others Pay Their Tolls and Tickets

text.headline: IOActive Jailbreaks Reviver Digital License Plates, Making Others Pay Tolls and Tickets
text.text:
Security researcher Josep Pi Rodriguez from security firm IOActive disclosed that Reviver's digital license plates contain security vulnerabilities that could allow them to be "jailbroken." The research showed that electronic license plates can bypass JTAG debug interface protection through fault injection attacks, thereby accessing firmware in on-chip Flash. Fault injection attacks require connecting wire harnesses to the internal chip of the license plate, monitoring voltage, and at specific moments disabling security features through "voltage glitching" to analyze and rewrite firmware. Attackers can achieve complete control of the electronic license plate by flashing custom firmware.

The researchers demonstrated that after flashing new firmware, they could use a mobile app to connect to the license plate via BLE and modify the displayed content. This attack method enables arbitrary changes to the license plate number, evading traffic tickets and tolls, and even shifting tickets to others. Not only can this be used to jailbreak one's own license plate, but it could also be used to target unsuspecting vehicle owners. If hackers, parking attendants, or auto mechanics could remove the license plate and install their own firmware, they could secretly track vehicle owners, and even remotely change the license plate number by connecting it to a hacker-controlled server.

Multiple U.S. states have legalized the purchase of digital license plates and allow their use nationwide. Compared to traditional metal license plates, digital plates offer advantages such as dynamic display, personalized customization, and vehicle status updates (e.g., marking as stolen). Reviver is the primary supplier of digital license plates and has sold approximately 65,000 plates.

media.caption: Attorney General Ken Paxton Sues General Motors for Unlawfully Collecting Drivers' Private Data and Selling It To Several Companies, Including Insurance Companies

text.headline: Texas Sues General Motors: Over 14 Million Vehicles Suspected of Collecting Driver Data
text.text:
General Motors was sued by the state of Texas, accused of installing technology in over 14 million vehicles to collect driver data and then selling that data to insurance companies and other companies without drivers' consent.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit against General Motors and its subsidiary OnStar, alleging that the two companies collected and sold private driving data of more than 1.8 million Texas residents to insurance companies without customers' knowledge or consent, violating data privacy regulations. The information was also sold to several other companies, including at least two companies that generated "driving scores" for General Motors customers.

The lawsuit stemmed from a June 2024 investigation into whether several automakers collected and sold large amounts of data without drivers' knowledge. When customers purchased vehicles, General Motors forced them to register through products like OnStar Smart Driver during the onboarding process, telling them that failure to register would result in deactivation of vehicle safety features. However, through registration, customers effectively "consented" to General Motors collecting and selling their data. Despite lengthy and complex disclosures, General Motors never informed customers of its actual practices — systematically collecting and selling their detailed driving data.

Through technology installed in 2015 and later model years, General Motors collected, recorded, analyzed, and transmitted extremely detailed driving data about each trip. The collected data was used to compile "driving scores" assessing whether the state's more than 1.8 million drivers had "bad habits" such as speeding, hard braking, aggressive cornering, not wearing seatbelts, and late-night driving. These scores were sold to insurance companies and other companies without drivers' consent. Insurance companies could use this data to decide whether to raise premiums, cancel policies, or deny coverage.

media.caption: Hacking Kia: Remotely Controlling Cars With Just a License Plate

text.headline: Remotely Controlling Any Kia Vehicle With Just a License Plate Number/VIN
text.text:
Security researchers discovered multiple vulnerabilities in Kia's dealer management system, enabling remote control of vehicles using only the VIN, including obtaining personal information and adding attackers as hidden users of the vehicle. Affected models include 2014-2025 CARNIVAL, K5, SELTOS, SORENTO, and others, totaling approximately 15.5 million vehicles.

The Kia dealer management system had identity management flaws that allowed generation of high-privilege dealer authentication credentials. Using the generated credentials, attackers could add themselves as the first owner of the vehicle, achieving vehicle takeover and remote control. The vehicle takeover process requires only 5 steps, with no notification sent to the owner during the process:
1. Send a request to generate dealer authentication credentials;
2. Query the owner's phone number or email via the VIN;
3. Use the email and VIN to downgrade the owner's permissions to add a new owner;
4. Add the attacker's email as the first user of the vehicle, completing the takeover;
5. Use the added account to track the vehicle, unlock it, start it, etc.

Taking over a specific vehicle only requires knowing the VIN, which can be viewed directly from outside the vehicle through the front windshield on the driver's side. Additionally, third-party APIs can be used to look up the VIN based on the license plate number.

text.headline: Volkswagen Group Hit by 8Base Ransomware Attack
text.text:
The 8Base ransomware gang claimed to have stolen a large number of documents from Volkswagen and threatened to publish them. LeMagIT editors confirmed with Volkswagen that a ransomware attack had occurred. A spokesperson stated, "The incident is known at this time, and Volkswagen Group's IT infrastructure is not affected. We will continue to closely monitor the situation."

On September 23, 8Base downloaded a large number of Volkswagen Group documents, and on September 26, publicly posted ransomware information on their website. The ransom payment deadline set by 8Base has now expired.

The group claimed to have stolen a large amount of confidential information, including:
· Invoices, receipts, and accounting vouchers
· Personal data
· Certificates
· Employee directories
· Large amounts of credential information
· Non-disclosure agreements
· Personal documents, etc.

media.caption: 0-click RCE on Tesla Model 3 through TPMS Sensors

text.headline: Synacktiv Discloses Tesla TPMS (Tire Pressure Monitoring System) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability Details at Hexacon
text.text:
Two security researchers from Synacktiv, David Berard & Thomas Imbert, shared their vulnerability details used to hack Tesla at PWN2OWN Automotive during the Hexacon security conference, titled "0-click RCE on Tesla Model 3 through TPMS Sensors."

TPMS sensors (Tire-Pressure Monitoring System) are used to monitor tire pressure and temperature and are mandatory requirements for vehicles to ensure safe driving. Earlier versions used 433 MHz radio; Tesla now uses low-power Bluetooth via BLE GATT characteristics.

Tesla's VCSEC ECU has an integer overflow vulnerability when processing x509 certificates. The issue stems from improper certificate parsing, with an integer overflow vulnerability during certificate fragment validation, leading to an out-of-bounds write (OOB write), which attackers can exploit to control program flow. This allows attackers to rewrite memory structures, control function pointers, and jump to malicious code.

Attackers need to forge a TPMS sensor and establish a connection with the VCSEC ECU via BLE broadcast messages, then send specially crafted certificate data to trigger the integer overflow vulnerability, control program flow, and ultimately execute arbitrary code. Subsequently, the vulnerability can be used to send CAN messages to control vehicle behavior, such as unlocking doors, starting the engine, applying brakes, etc.

media.caption: 0-click RCE on the IVI component: Pwn2Own Automotive edition

text.headline: PCAutomotive Discloses Alpine Halo9 iLX-F509 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability Details at Hexacon 2024
text.text:
Security researcher Mikhail Evdokimov (@konatabrk) from PCAutomotive shared the technical details of their exploitation of the Alpine Halo9 infotainment system during PWN2OWN Automotive at the Hexacon security conference, titled "0-click RCE on the IVI component: Pwn2Own Automotive edition." A UAF vulnerability exists in the Bluetooth protocol stack, enabling arbitrary code execution without any user interaction.

CVE-2024-23923: Alpine Halo9 prh_l2_sar_data_ind contains a Use-After-Free remote code execution vulnerability. This vulnerability allows a network-adjacent attacker to execute arbitrary code on affected Alpine Halo9 devices.

media.caption: Notice of Ransomware Attack Incident

text.headline: Japanese Auto Parts Supplier YOROZU Confirms Ransomware Attack
text.text:
On October 23, Japanese automotive parts supplier YOROZU confirmed it had suffered a ransomware attack. The attack resulted in the encryption of files stored on some of YOROZU's servers and the exfiltration of 849GB of data, including confidential documents related to automakers such as Nissan, Honda, and Toyota.

Founded in 1948, YOROZU was initially part of the Nissan Group, specializing in the production of automotive chassis suspension systems, supplying parts to multiple automakers including Nissan, General Motors, Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Fuji Heavy Industries, Suzuki, Mitsubishi, Ford, Hino, and Renault.

In a statement, the company said the attack was first discovered on October 14, when multiple files were encrypted and could not be accessed normally. YOROZU immediately established a cybersecurity incident response team to investigate and isolated the infected servers from the internet and internal network.

The ransomware group RansomHub claimed responsibility for the attack and stated it had successfully exfiltrated 849GB of confidential data, including contracts, technical documents, budget reports, production technology, accounting files, insurance records, human resources files, databases, and development documents related to its partner automakers.

media.caption: Multiple Vulnerabilities in the Mazda In-Vehicle Infotainment (IVI) System

text.headline: ZDI Discloses Multiple Vulnerabilities in Mazda Infotainment System
text.text:
ZDI security researcher Dmitry Janushkevich discovered multiple high-severity vulnerabilities in the CMU (CONNECTIVITY MASTER UNIT) infotainment head unit used in multiple Mazda models, affecting vehicles including 2014-2021 Mazda3. The CMU head unit is manufactured by Visteon, with the initial software version developed by Johnson Controls. The CMU system consists of two parts: a SoC and a VIP MCU, with the SoC running Linux and the VIP MCU using an unknown RTOS.

Attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities by constructing specially crafted USB devices (such as an iPod or mass storage device) and connecting them to the target system. Successful exploitation of some of these vulnerabilities allows arbitrary code execution with root privileges. These vulnerabilities affect the latest software version (74.00.324A) and below. The supplier has not yet patched these vulnerabilities.
· CVE-2024-8355: An iAP serial number SQL injection vulnerability in DeviceManager, allowing SQL injection attacks via connected Apple devices, which can tamper with the database with root privileges and even achieve arbitrary code execution. Since the input length is limited to 0x36 bytes, exploitation of this vulnerability is somewhat restricted, but this can be overcome by connecting several spoofed iPods one after another, each injecting its own SQL statement in place of the serial number.
· CVE-2024-8356: The MCU update program does not validate the legitimacy of flash packages, allowing updates with unsigned flash packages, which enables attackers to move laterally from the Linux-running SoC to the MCU, achieving direct access to the CAN bus and sending arbitrary CAN messages.
· CVE-2024-8357: The application SoC running Linux lacks a hardware root of trust, allowing attackers to manipulate the root file system, configuration data, and boot code for persistence, SSH key installation, and code execution.
· CVE-2024-8358, CVE-2024-8359, CVE-2024-8360 are command injection vulnerabilities due to insufficient input filtering during system update processing. For example, command injection can be achieved through filenames of update files ending in .up.

ZDI stated that this attack can be completed in minutes in a laboratory environment and would not take much longer in the real world, such as when a car is "handled by valets, during carpooling, or through USB malware execution." Once the CMU is compromised, further attacks can be launched through it. For example, attempting to attack any connected device in a targeted attack, resulting in DoS, destruction, ransomware, functional safety impacts, etc.

media.caption: Multiple vulnerabilities in Enel X JuiceBox (Waybox) Pro & Plus 3.0 charger

text.headline: PCAutomotive Discloses Multiple Vulnerabilities in Enel X JuiceBox Wall-Mounted EV Charger
text.text:
PCAutomotive discovered multiple vulnerabilities that could allow potential attackers to gain root privileges on the Enel X JuiceBox (Waybox) Pro and Plus 3.0 wall-mounted EV charger operating system. After gaining root privileges, attackers could access sensitive data stored on the charger, bypass charging limits set by the device owner, cause charger denial of service, and modify firmware.

· CVE-2023-29114: System log leakage. The log page /admin/log.php contains Wi-Fi credentials, APN addresses and credentials, IPSEC credentials, web management console login credentials, C2G configuration, and other sensitive information.
· CVE-2023-29115: Denial of service via the web management interface. Accessing /admin/reboot.php reboots the charger.
· CVE-2023-29116: PHP information leakage. Accessing /admin/phpinfo.php reveals PHP version, server environment variables, and other information.
· CVE-2023-29117: Authentication bypass. After accessing /api/command.php?action=set_param&param=adminPasswordVisible&values=True, the plaintext password appears on the homepage login form.
· CVE-2023-29118, CVE-2023-29119: Unauthenticated SQLite injection.
· CVE-2023-29120: Unauthenticated command injection in the ssid parameter of wifi_check.
· CVE-2023-29121: Exposed TCF proxy service. Port 1534 serves as an Eclipse debug interface, allowing attackers to debug programs, modify the file system, and obtain a root shell.
· CVE-2023-29122: Incorrect file ownership of privileged service libraries. CM_main.exe runs with root privileges, while the used shared libraries are owned by user and group daemon.
· CVE-2023-29125: CM_main.exe listens on port 7700. A message body length greater than 0x20000 causes a heap overflow.
· CVE-2023-29126: Insecure loose comparison. Loose comparison (==) is used for password comparison, e.g., 0 equals 0e1234. This reduces the complexity of password cracking for attackers.

These vulnerabilities affect firmware versions prior to 2.1.1.0_JB3VU096A. Each charger has a web management console that can be accessed via Wi-Fi connection or the Ethernet port below the front panel. The default password for the management console can be found in the security manual on the Enel X website.

media.caption: Over the Air: Compromise of Modern Volkswagen Group Vehicles

text.headline: PCAutomotive Discloses Multiple Vulnerabilities in Volkswagen MIB3 Infotainment System at Black Hat Europe
text.text:
Automotive security firm PCAutomotive disclosed 12 security vulnerabilities affecting the latest Skoda Superb III sedan at Black Hat Europe. PCAutomotive had previously disclosed 9 medium and low severity vulnerabilities for this model on November 22, 2023. This time, multiple high-severity vulnerabilities were disclosed, including picserver integer overflow and heap overflow, BL2 secure boot bypass, command injection in network services, lack of access control mechanisms, and plaintext storage of phonebook contacts.

These vulnerabilities exist in the Skoda Superb III's MIB3 infotainment unit, which is widely used across multiple Volkswagen Group models, covering functions including Bluetooth connectivity, GPS navigation, entertainment audio, and communication synchronization. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities enables unrestricted code execution and running malicious code each time the unit starts. This allows attackers to obtain the vehicle's real-time GPS location and speed data, record in-cabin conversations (via the in-vehicle microphone), capture screenshots of the in-vehicle display, and even play arbitrary sounds inside the vehicle. Attackers only need to connect to the Skoda Superb III's media unit via Bluetooth to exploit these vulnerabilities.

The vulnerable MIB3 infotainment units not only affect the Skoda Superb III but are also widely used in multiple other Volkswagen and Skoda brand models. Based on public sales data, PCAutomotive estimates that over 1.4 million vehicles on the market may have similar security risks.

After learning of these vulnerabilities, Volkswagen took remediation measures and released relevant security patches. Volkswagen stated that the vulnerabilities have been resolved through the cybersecurity disclosure program and that owners' safety and vehicle driving functions were not threatened.

text.headline: Financial Investigation: Exploiting "Smart Parking" System Vulnerabilities to Locate Vehicles — Uncovering the Vehicle Tracking Black Industry Chain
text.text:
With the acceleration of smart city development, smart parking, as an innovative service model, has played a positive role in improving urban traffic management efficiency and enhancing citizen travel experiences. However, a recent report by CCTV Finance exposed personal information security issues in smart parking systems, drawing widespread social attention.

During the smart parking process, when a vehicle enters or exits a parking lot, the system automatically records data such as the vehicle's entry and exit times, license plate number, and parking location. This data serves as the foundational information for parking lot operators to optimize space allocation and billing settlement. Parking information includes the complete closed loop of a vehicle entering and leaving a specific location, constituting location tracking information classified as sensitive personal information under the Personal Information Protection Law. However, according to CCTV's investigation, criminals can even input a license plate number from a remote distance and easily obtain key information such as the parking lot where the vehicle is located and entry time without any identity verification, effectively leaving vehicle owners "exposed" in the digital world. Once obtained by malicious actors, this could lead to threats to personal safety, financial losses, and other serious consequences.

Reporters learned that criminals exploited data interface vulnerabilities in "smart parking" systems to crack parking lot databases. They first took orders via the internet to help clients locate specific vehicles. Once a target vehicle entered a parking lot within the compromised range, they would relay real-time parking information to downstream vehicle-tracking groups. Within minutes, a tracker would accept the order and head directly to the parking lot, photograph the vehicle information, and covertly attach a GPS tracker to a hidden location on the target vehicle. According to police records, the trackers and the upstream criminals who breached the parking data systems profited significantly.

text.headline: CCC Discloses: Volkswagen Exposes 800,000 Vehicles' Data on the Public Internet Due to Misconfiguration
text.text:
At the 38th Chaos Computer Club (CCC) Congress, CCC security analyst Flüpke and journalist Michael Kreil disclosed that a massive amount of Volkswagen data was exposed on the public internet. Volkswagen Group subsidiary CARIAD stored detailed operational data and large amounts of owner information for 807,357 electric vehicles in Amazon Cloud. The access credentials for this data could be obtained without authorization. The data included over 15 million vehicle identification numbers, models, manufacturing years, countries/regions, and user IDs; over 600,000 user records including user IDs, names, emails, mobile phone numbers, and dates of birth; and 9.5TB of vehicle status data including location coordinate data.

The location data could be accurate to within 10 centimeters, thereby exposing individuals' movement trajectories and other more sensitive behavioral data. This vulnerability enabled extremely precise tracking of users' whereabouts. Der Spiegel's report demonstrated the trajectory leaks of two German political figures. A member of the German Defense Committee had his movements tracked to his father's nursing home and German military bases, while a mayor's vehicle recorded her trajectory from city hall to her therapist's office. The report also included information on 35 electric vehicles belonging to the Hamburg Police Department, other political figures, business leaders, and some drivers associated with the U.S. Air Force Ramstein Air Base.

The root cause of the data breach was that the server's SpringBoot Heapdump (memory dump) could be obtained without authorization, containing AWS (Amazon Cloud) access credentials. This created a risk of data leakage for the large amounts of data stored there. The affected data covered vehicles from Volkswagen, SEAT, Audi, and Skoda brands.

After Cariad and Volkswagen Group headquarters received CCC's notification, they responded within hours, without even attempting to downplay the severity of the incident. The vulnerability has been fixed, and unauthorized personnel can no longer access the data.

media.caption: Mercedes-Benz Head Unit security research report

text.headline: Kaspersky Discloses Multiple Vulnerabilities in Mercedes-Benz Head Unit
text.text:
Russian cybersecurity firm Kaspersky published a blog post providing an in-depth analysis of the Mercedes-Benz User Experience (MBUX) system's anti-theft system, firmware unpacking, IPC, internal network, and USB functions. This research primarily targeted the first-generation MBUX system. Kaspersky described its research findings in detail and released security advisories for each vulnerability. A total of 13 CVE numbers were obtained, and details of some vulnerabilities were disclosed.

The test environment included a Mercedes-Benz B180 and a test bench. When building the test bench, it was discovered that the head unit would trigger anti-theft mode. The anti-theft state could be reset by periodically sending specific CAN messages. MBUX consists of MMB (Multi Media Board), BB (Base Board), CSB (Country Specific Board), and RH850. By removing the storage chip, the MMB firmware was extracted from the eMMC. Additionally, firmware could be obtained from the diagnostic tool website using specific hardware part numbers. Some older firmware versions could be found online, with some of the data encrypted. These files could be decrypted using shared libraries built into the diagnostic tool. Furthermore, automotive suppliers could still use diagnostic tools for offline updates.

The head unit defines multiple IPC types (thriftme/MoCCA/GCF)
· CVE-2024-37600: MoCCA is developed based on the DSI framework and uses HTTP protocol for data transmission. The disconnect parameter passed via POST has a stack overflow.
· CVE-2023-34404: Command injection vulnerability in the MAC address parameter passed to the system function via the GCF protocol for iptables execution.
· Privilege escalation using a historical Polkit vulnerability (CVE-2021-4034).

Using QEMU to emulate the USB subsystem, DeviceManager handles USB events such as adding, removing, and mounting. GDVariantCodingService is used to identify head unit and vehicle parameters for other services. The head unit supports importing and exporting user profile files (seat positions, favorite radio channels, etc.) via USB, with the service provided by CSystemProfileServiceImpl.
· CVE-2024-37601: A heap overflow vulnerability in the process of decoding files with the extension *.ud2. UserData encodes data via CHBString, and CHBString::const_iterator::incrementSteps incorrectly handles the character with code 0xe7, parsing 3 bytes from UTF8LookUpTable as 1 byte. Without further exploitation, triggering the vulnerability during data import causes the system to enter a frozen state that can only be resolved through ECU hard reset.
· CVE-2023-34402: vt_ab.xml contains descriptions of which services are dropped during processing. Due to lack of validation, attackers can control the path of content written by the "UserDataExchangeServiceClient::unpackVoiceTagArchiveOptimized" service.
· CVE-2023-34399: Integer overflow vulnerability in the boost library 1.81 used in processing the uapreds.db SQLite data

media.caption: Hacking Subaru: Tracking and Controlling Cars via the STARLINK Admin Panel

text.headline: Subaru STARLINK Admin Panel Vulnerable to Arbitrary Account Takeover, Enabling Vehicle Tracking and Control
text.text:
Security researchers Sam Curry and Shubham Shah discovered an authentication flaw in Subaru's STARLINK connected vehicle service, enabling unrestricted access to all vehicles and user accounts in the U.S., Canada, and Japan.

Through subdomain scanning, they discovered the STARLINK Admin Portal (https://portal.prod.subarucs.com/login.html). Analysis of /assets/_js/ revealed a flaw in the password reset authentication function. The password reset endpoint /forgotPassword/resetPassword.json did not validate employee password reset credentials, allowing direct password resets. Additionally, another endpoint /adminProfile/getSecurityQuestion.json?email=example@example.com could be used to enumerate employee emails and obtain valid email addresses on the platform. Combining the two vulnerabilities, the researchers obtained valid employee email addresses through enumeration, then used the arbitrary password reset vulnerability to complete account takeover and successfully log into the admin panel. Although the admin panel had 2FA (two-factor authentication), it was only frontend validation. After removing the blocking page on the frontend, the platform's functions could be used to monitor vehicle trajectories, control vehicles, and obtain user data. Employees could access large amounts of user data without triggering any alerts.

With only the victim's last name, zip code, email address, phone number, or license plate number, an attacker could:
· Start, stop, unlock, lock, and obtain the current location of any vehicle;
· Query the location history of any vehicle for the past year;
· Query any user's personally identifiable information, including emergency contacts, authorized users, physical addresses, billing information, and vehicle PIN.
· Access other user data, including support call history, previous owners, odometer readings, and sales history.

After reporting the vulnerabilities, the affected systems were patched within 24 hours, with no evidence of malicious exploitation.

media.caption: Double Tap at the Blackbox: Hacking a Car Remotely Twice with MiTM

text.headline: Man-in-the-Middle Attack Used to Compromise 3 XPeng Vehicle Models
text.text:
Security researchers Cao Yingjie from 360 and Xinfeng Chen from SigVoid presented at Black Hat Asia 2025, disclosing their security research findings on XPeng vehicles. They achieved vehicle control twice through man-in-the-middle attacks.

1. The "Game Center" uses an insecure HTTP channel for updates. By hijacking the update traffic and replacing the app, they obtained lower application privileges. Then they extracted other applications and reverse-engineered the method to open engineering mode via the dial pad. They used CVE-2015-1805 for privilege escalation, then reverse-engineered Car Control to achieve vehicle control.

2. Some in-vehicle Android apps use self-signed SSL communication and trust user-installed certificates. Since certificate validation was not properly implemented, all server certificates were trusted, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on encrypted communication. By conducting ARP attacks within the same network segment and using mitmproxy for man-in-the-middle attacks, they captured and tampered with MQTT messages controlling the vehicle, achieving vehicle control.

text.headline: Security Team Discloses: Numerous Dashcams Contain Critical Vulnerabilities
text.text:
HE&T Security Lab jointly with Global Tech Company presented at Black Hat Asia 2025. They conducted systematic security research on 24 dashcam models from 15 brands, discovering and exploiting dozens of vulnerabilities and successfully compromising over 20 mainstream devices. The researchers documented the complete attack process, including device discovery, pairing bypass, audio/video and GPS data extraction, road sign and location information extraction, and even further analysis using large language models.

Key vulnerabilities identified include: device pairing bypass (e.g., MAC address spoofing), default or hardcoded Wi-Fi passwords, unauthenticated HTTP services, mobile app vulnerabilities, file upload vulnerabilities, and private port file exposure.

In vulnerability exploitation demonstrations, the research team obtained access through file upload vulnerabilities, brute-forced the root password, successfully modified system configurations such as disabling battery protection, changing fixed passwords, disabling audio/video recording and watermark features, and lateral movement to control vehicles. Affected brands include Hikvision, THINKWARE, Audi, BMW, BLACKVUE, 70mai, IROAD, etc., highlighting the widespread shortcomings in design and security protection of current dashcams.

media.caption: Remote Exploitation of Nissan Leaf: Controlling Critical Body Elements from the Internet

text.headline: PCAutomotive Presents at Black Hat Asia 2025, Discloses Multiple Nissan Leaf Vulnerabilities
text.text:
PCAutomotive security researchers Radu Motspan, Mikhail Evdokimov, Polina Smirnov, and others presented their security research on the Nissan Leaf ZE1 2020 model at Black Hat Asia 2025, disclosing multiple vulnerabilities. Their research focused on the infotainment system, supplied by Bosch, with the SoC using NXP IMX6, the MCU using Renesas RH850, and the Wi-Fi+Bluetooth module provided by Alps Alpine.

Starting from a Bluetooth vulnerability, they achieved a multi-stage attack chain, ultimately achieving complete control over CAN bus commands. Multiple stack overflow vulnerabilities exist in the Bluetooth HFP (Hands-Free Profile) stack, enabling arbitrary command execution by constructing ROP chains to call system(). Persistence was achieved through SSHD and secure boot bypass respectively. By reverse-engineering Bosch open-source code, they determined the CAN message structure sent from the SoC to the MCU, and discovered a stack overflow on the MCU to achieve arbitrary code execution.

· CVE-2025-32056: Anti-theft bypass
· CVE-2025-32057: app_redbend man-in-the-middle attack
· CVE-2025-32058: V850 stack overflow during CBR processing
· CVE-2025-32059: Stack overflow leading to RCE [0]
· CVE-2025-32060: Kernel signature verification region missing
· CVE-2025-32061: Stack overflow leading to RCE [1]
· CVE-2025-32062: Stack overflow leading to RCE [2]
· PCA_NISSAN_009: Improper filtering between IT CAN and other CAN traffic
· CVE-2025-32063: Persistence in Wi-Fi network
· PCA_NISSAN_012: Persistence achieved by exploiting CVE-2017-7932 (discovered by Quarkslab, stack overflow in secure boot CSF signature process) in i.MX 6 HAB

text.headline: IVECO (China) Official Website Search Engine Results Show Pornographic Content

text.headline: Security Researcher Discloses Multiple Vulnerabilities in KIA RTOS Head Unit System
text.text:
At the Hardwear.io USA 2025/Defcon 33 security conference, researcher Danilo Erazo disclosed severe vulnerabilities in the RTOS head unit MOTREX MTXNC10AB system used in multiple KIA models (KIA Soluto/Pegas/Picanto, etc.). Issues include weak validation, incomplete firmware integrity protection, private key leakage, use of outdated libraries, and insecure Bluetooth pairing. These defects could lead to firmware tampering, persistent backdoors, privacy leakage, and communication hijacking, posing significant threats to vehicle safety. The research also demonstrated replacing QR code images in the firmware's maintenance manual with phishing links to achieve malicious redirection, demonstrating the risk of head units being backdoored and combined with social engineering attacks.

· The Bootloader uses only a 1-byte CRC checksum, providing insufficient validation strength.
· Firmware integrity verification does not cover all binary files, creating bypass risks.
· Dependent third-party libraries MattrixSSL 3.7 and libpng 1.2.29 have known vulnerabilities.
· The head unit stores communication and signing private keys in plaintext, which if obtained could decrypt communication traffic and sign malicious update packages.
· Bluetooth PIN code is recorded in plaintext in UART logs.
· The head unit forces the use of insecure Bluetooth Legacy Pairing.

The company emphasized it is continuously evaluating all available information and will report the matter to law enforcement agencies if necessary. media.caption: PerfektBlue
media.credit: PerfektBlue - critical vulnerabilities in OpenSynergy Blue SDK A chain of 4 vulnerabilities in Blue SDK Bluetooth stack leading to 1-click RCE

text.headline: PerfektBlue: OpenSynergy BlueSDK Contains Critical Bluetooth Vulnerability Attack Chain
text.text:
Security firm PCA Cyber Security disclosed PerfektBlue, a critical Bluetooth air-interface attack chain with broad impact, affecting millions of devices in the automotive and other industries. The attack chain exploits multiple vulnerabilities in OpenSynergy's BlueSDK Bluetooth protocol stack. Four exploitable vulnerabilities exist in BlueSDK that can be chained together, requiring only a single click by the target user to execute the attack. Once these vulnerabilities are successfully exploited, attackers can achieve remote code execution on the target device.
·CVE-2024-45434: UAF vulnerability in AVRCP service;
·CVE-2024-45431: Improper L2CAP CID validation;
·CVE-2024-45432: Function call with incorrect parameters in RFCOMM protocol;
·CVE-2024-45433: Function not properly terminated in RFCOMM protocol.

Using PerfektBlue, researchers successfully obtained Bluetooth application shell access on the Volkswagen ID.4, Mercedes-Benz NTG6&NTG7, and Skoda Superb in-vehicle infotainment systems.

Although BlueSDK is also used in other domains (such as phones and portable devices), most potentially affected devices are in the automotive sector. Researchers used publicly available Bluetooth certification information resources to identify manufacturers and products using the BlueSDK framework. Some affected manufacturers include: Mercedes-Benz (Mercedes-Benz AG), Volkswagen, and Skoda. If an attacker achieves code execution in the in-vehicle infotainment system (IVI), they could: track vehicle GPS location;
listen to in-cabin audio; steal personal information such as phonebooks; and move laterally to attack other electronic control units (ECUs). Whether through legitimate interfaces or further vulnerability exploitation, attackers could ultimately gain control over critical vehicle systems.

media.caption: Remote Code Execution Discovered in XTool AnyScan App: Risks to Phones and Vehicles

text.headline: Well-Known Auto Diagnostic Tool Manufacturer XTool's AnyScan App Contains Remote Code Execution Vulnerability: Threatening Phone and Vehicle Security
text.text:
XTOOL is an automotive intelligent diagnostics brand under Shenzhen Yunjia Intelligent. AnyScan is an automotive diagnostic application running on Android phones by XTOOL, supporting remote vehicle diagnostics via an OBD-II adapter. XTool AnyScan has been downloaded over 50,000 times on the Google Play Store.

Security firm NowSecure discovered that XTool's AnyScan Android app version 4.40.11 has serious design flaws in its update mechanism, encryption, and communication. Attackers can exploit the insecure plugin update feature to deliver malicious code through man-in-the-middle attacks, control the user's phone, and further send malicious CAN commands to the vehicle. This vulnerability not only endangers mobile device security but could also lead to remote vehicle manipulation, threatening user privacy and driving safety.
· Insecure update mechanism: In-app plugin updates bypass Google Play review and lack signature verification.
· Missing TLS validation: Custom TrustManager accepts all certificates, allowing attackers to spoof servers and hijack traffic.
· Weak encryption and hardcoded values: Update data uses DES 56-bit algorithm, with keys and IV hardcoded, making them easy to decrypt and tamper with.
· Update integrity deficiency: Only MD5 is provided but not actually verified, allowing malicious plugin replacement.

· At the phone level, the app has sensitive permissions including camera, GPS, Bluetooth, and file system access. After successful exploitation, attackers can obtain sensitive information.
· At the vehicle level, through OBD-II interface interaction with the vehicle bus, malicious code can send dangerous CAN commands, leading to risks such as unlocking doors and engine control.

On June 10, 2025, NowSecure informed XTOOL Technology of the vulnerabilities, and received confirmation on July 11. However, as of NowSecure's disclosure (July 16), the vulnerabilities still existed in the latest version of AnyScan 4.40.40. NowSecure recommends uninstalling AnyScan and waiting for a secure version after the vulnerabilities are fixed.

media.caption: Tracking the Tractors: Analyzing Smart Farming Automation Systems for Fun and Profit

text.headline: FJDynamics Smart Agricultural Machinery Autonomous Driving System Contains Critical Vulnerabilities: Tens of Thousands of Tractors Can Be Remotely Compromised and Controlled
text.text:
Researchers Felix Eberstaller and Bernhard Rader from LIMES Security disclosed at Black Hat USA 2025 that FJDynamics' smart agricultural machinery autonomous driving system contains critical vulnerabilities, allowing tens of thousands of tractors worldwide to be remotely compromised and controlled.

The researchers found that the smart agricultural machinery uses an MQTT cloud platform and an Android tablet as the human-machine interface, lacking basic security protection. Attackers can intercept and decrypt MQTT communications, impersonate any tractor to connect to the cloud, obtain farmer locations, land information, and equipment operating status, and even remotely issue lock commands to disable equipment. The system's OTA updates do not enable TLS or signature verification, enabling attackers to achieve remote code execution through man-in-the-middle attacks and fully take over equipment. The vulnerabilities can also be used to manipulate steering systems, tamper with GPS data, and steal farmer privacy, affecting agricultural critical infrastructure security.

· The TLS used by MQTT does not verify server legitimacy; a self-signed certificate can hijack encrypted MQTT communication.
· MQTT access control is missing; using /# allows subscribing to all Topics, obtaining messages from other vehicles, and even publishing messages to remotely lock vehicles, send notifications, etc.
· The in-vehicle Android tablet is designed to only use the FJDynamics app, but can be escaped to the native system.
· APK upgrades are transmitted in plaintext with only MD5 integrity verification and no legitimacy verification. Through man-in-the-middle app replacement, Root privileges were obtained.
· The vehicle control protocol on the Android tablet was successfully reverse-engineered, sending commands via serial port ttyS0 to the ECU for steering wheel control.

media.caption: Smart Bus Smart Hacking: From Free WiFi to Total Control
media.credit: Gateways to Chaos - How We Proved Modems Are a Ticking Time Bomb That Hackers Can Access Everywhere

text.headline: Smart Bus Hacking Attack: From Free Wi-Fi to Total Control
text.text:
Researcher Chiao-Lin Yu (Steven Meow) (Trend Micro Taiwan) and Kai-Ching 'Keniver' Wang (CHT Security) disclosed at DEFCON 33 that Taiwan's smart bus system contains critical vulnerabilities allowing attackers to remotely compromise vehicles.

The free Wi-Fi provided on a certain bus. Analysis revealed that the onboard M2M router (Billion M120N) simultaneously handles passenger Wi-Fi and the vehicle's core systems (APTS, ADAS) without network isolation. After bypassing router authentication to access the backend, researchers discovered multiple vulnerabilities, including command injection. Attackers can locate and remotely attack buses over the internet, subsequently accessing sensitive data such as GPS location, engine RPM, average vehicle speed, and camera video feeds. They can also tamper with display screens, trigger false alarms, steal passenger and driver information, and even disrupt bus operations. The protocols used lack encryption and authentication, making the system highly susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks, endangering public transportation safety.

media.caption: How a vulnerability in obscure dealer software could have unlocked your car from anywhere

text.headline: API Vulnerability Exposes Over 1,000 US Dealerships and Vehicles to Remote Control
text.text:
Security researcher Eaton Zveare disclosed at DEFCON 33 that a major automaker's dealer platform contains critical vulnerabilities affecting over 1,000 dealerships across the United States, allowing attackers to remotely take over vehicle control.

The centralized dealer system is used for vehicle ordering, sales, customer management, and vehicle binding. The researcher discovered flaws in registration and permission verification, enabling the creation of national-level administrator accounts to access and control all dealer functions. Attackers can use this entry point to obtain consumer private information, locate target vehicles via VIN or name, and abuse the dealer's vehicle owner binding system to forcibly transfer vehicles to their own accounts, enabling remote vehicle start, door unlocking, and location tracking.

A hidden registration form was first discovered, and by modifying the web frontend, the registration form was displayed normally. Since the server did not verify registered user credentials, accounts could be created freely. Initially, created accounts required approval before use, and the system's verification mechanism blocked further operations. Subsequently, a JavaScript script for administrator user management was discovered. By modifying the JS script to bypass local authentication, a "national administrator" account was successfully created.

media.caption: WikileaksV2-Nissan CBI

text.headline: Nissan Breached by Ransomware, 4TB of Core Data Stolen
text.text:
Japanese automaker Nissan confirmed that its subsidiary Creative Box Inc. (CBI) experienced a data breach involving core vehicle design materials. The attack was carried out by the Qilin ransomware group, which claimed to have stolen 4TB of data across 405,882 files, including 3D full vehicle design models, internal reports, financial documents, virtual reality (VR) design processes, and vehicle photographs.

CBI, headquartered in Tokyo and a subsidiary of Nissan Motor, is a "think tank" design studio specializing in experimental and concept vehicle design.

A Nissan spokesperson stated that on August 16, CBI detected suspicious access activity on its data servers and immediately took emergency measures, including severing server access and promptly reporting to the police.

On August 20, Qilin listed CBI on its dark web ransom portal, claiming to have obtained all design project data and threatening to publish the information to benefit competitors if the ransom was not paid. Qilin also displayed several photos of stolen files on the dark web, including vehicle 3D renderings, spreadsheets, internal documents, and automotive interior design images.

Nissan emphasized that this leak only involved the company's own data and would not affect other customers, contractors, or third-party companies.

media.caption: Statement on Cyber Incident

text.headline: Jaguar Land Rover Suffers Cyberattack Causing Production Halt, 33,000 Employees Forced on Leave
text.text:
On September 2, 2025, Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), a British automaker under India's Tata Motors, disclosed that its global production operations had suffered a severe cyberattack, causing core production system outages, forcing multiple factories to halt production, and temporarily furloughing some employees.
JLR confirmed that attackers had stolen some data and had reported the data breach to relevant regulatory authorities.

The incident had a broad impact, with production lines in Slovakia, China, India, and Brazil completely halted, and factories in the UK Midlands and Merseyside also stopping production. The supply chain was severely affected as well: some parts suppliers were unable to access JLR's ordering system, causing operational standstills, and companies exclusively supplying JLR such as Evtec and WHS Plastics were forced to suspend operations. Dealerships and repair shops were also impacted, with the digital parts ordering platform paralyzed, causing delays in customer vehicle repairs.

The cybercrime syndicate "Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters" (comprising Shiny Hunters, Lapsus$, and Scattered Spider) claimed responsibility for the attack and published screenshots of JLR's internal SAP system in Telegram groups. External observers speculated that the attackers may have exploited known vulnerabilities in SAP NetWeaver (CVE-2025-31324, CVE-2025-42999) to gain entry.

media.caption: Pwn My Ride: Exploring the CarPlay Attack Surface
media.credit: irborne: Wormable Zero-Click Remote Code Execution (RCE) in AirPlay Protocol Puts Apple & IoT Devices at Risk

text.headline: Apple CarPlay Can Be Remotely Controlled to Interfere with Driver Operations and Conduct Surveillance
text.text:
Researchers from security firm Oligo Security further disclosed details of Apple CarPlay vulnerabilities affecting a large number of vehicles at DEFCON 33. Previously, on April 29, a series of vulnerabilities in the AirPlay protocol stack named Airborne had already been disclosed.

CVE-2025-24132 is a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Airborne suite affecting CarPlay. This vulnerability allows attackers to execute arbitrary code (RCE) on CarPlay via USB or network access, potentially further penetrating the in-vehicle network, threatening in-vehicle communications, personal privacy data, and even affecting vehicle safety functions.

The attack targets the iAP2 protocol used by CarPlay to establish wireless connections. iAP2 employs one-way authentication, where the phone authenticates the in-vehicle infotainment system (head unit), but the head unit does not authenticate the phone. That is, the vehicle checks whether it is communicating with a legitimate device, but the device accepts any client using iAP2. An attacker with a Bluetooth radio device and a compatible iAP2 client can impersonate an iPhone, request Wi-Fi credentials, trigger application launches, and issue any iAP2 commands. Once the attacker completes the Bluetooth pairing process, they can authenticate via iAP2, obtain Wi-Fi credentials, and connect to the vehicle's hotspot. By combining this with CVE-2025-24132, remote arbitrary code execution is achieved. An attacker who successfully exploits this vulnerability can steal vehicle location data, eavesdrop on call contents, and even interfere with driver operations.

The vulnerability affects devices using AirPlay Audio SDK versions prior to 2.7.1, AirPlay Video SDK versions prior to 3.6.0.126, and CarPlay Communication Plugin R18.1 and earlier versions. Apple patched CVE-2025-24132 at the end of April, but only a few vendors have integrated the patch into their products to date.

media.caption: Technical Advisory: Tesla Telematics Control Unit - ADB Auth Bypass

text.headline: CVE-2025-34251: Tesla TCU ADB Authentication Bypass
text.text:
On September 29, security researchers Alex Plaskett and McCaulay Hudson from security firm NCC Group disclosed an ADB authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2025-34251) in Tesla's Telematics Control Unit (TCU/TBOX). The vulnerability affects firmware versions prior to 2025.14. With physical access, the ADB locking mechanism in production environments can be bypassed through the TCU's externally exposed Micro USB interface, ultimately gaining root privileges on the TCU.

Although the ADB shell has implemented access control, the adb push/pull functions are not authenticated, allowing unauthorized users to upload and download files. The ADB enable and lock mechanisms are defined in /etc/launch_adbd. When the state file /sys/class/qtee/secboot_state does not exist or the simulated file /data/dummy_auth_enable exists, it is locked; when auth_disable is present in /sys/class/qtee/secboot_state, it is unlocked. When /sys/class/qtee/secboot_state exists but does not contain auth_disable, authentication is required for use.

The steps to obtain a root shell are as follows:
1. Connect to the TCU via Micro USB
2. Add udev rules to identify the adb device. Write SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="2c7c", ATTR{idProduct}=="0452", MODE="0666", GROUP="plugdev" to /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules
3. Since most partitions are mounted as read-only, the directories where files can be written are limited. Abuse the uevent_helper/hotplug sysfs kernel subsystems to execute arbitrary commands, start a telnet service, and obtain a root shell. The specific method is to use adb push to upload the telnet startup script to /tmp/telnetd.sh on the TCU; then use adb push to upload t2.sh (containing /tmp/telnetd.sh) to /sys/kernel/uevent_helper and /proc/sys/kernel/hotplug on the TCU respectively; then use adb pull to read /etc/passwd to trigger a uevent; finally, enable adb forwarding, connect to the telnet service port, and obtain a root shell.

Tesla addressed this issue in subsequent versions. The fix includes disabling ADB listening on the Micro USB interface by default, and during the boot process, determining based on the two conditions /usr/bin/is-not-fused and /usr/bin/is-fa-build, allowing ADB to be enabled only in specific internal build scenarios, thereby preventing production vehicles from accessing debug functionality through physical interfaces.

media.caption: Grand Theft Auto: Gaining Control Over Tens of Thousands of Vehicles Through a Supply Chain Attack
media.credit: Critical Security Vulnerability in Vehicle Systems: Kaspersky Discovers Vulnerabilities Threatening Vehicle Safety

text.headline: Kaspersky Discloses Critical Vulnerability at SAS25 Allowing Full Control of Connected Vehicles Through Supply Chain Attack
text.text:
At the Security Analyst Summit (SAS) 25, Artem Zinenko, head of Kaspersky ICS CERT (Industrial Control Systems Cyber Emergency Response Team), disclosed a highly significant connected vehicle security research finding. During a remote security audit of an automaker, they discovered that attackers could progressively compromise the automaker's telematics system by exploiting a single zero-day vulnerability in a publicly accessible web application within the contractor's infrastructure, ultimately gaining control over a large number of connected vehicles.

Initial access was obtained by exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the contractor's publicly accessible web application, followed by credential theft and lateral movement to the automaker's telematics system. Due to issues such as misconfigured firewalls, weak passwords, and lack of two-factor authentication, the attack chain continued to expand. Ultimately, attackers were able to abuse the telematics platform's firmware update mechanism to push tampered firmware to the vehicle's Telematics Control Unit (TCU) and access the CAN bus, thereby achieving remote manipulation of critical systems such as the engine and transmission.
1. Contractor Web Application Zero-Day Vulnerability: Kaspersky discovered a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the contractor's externally accessible Wiki application. Through this vulnerability, researchers successfully exported the system user list and password hashes. Due to weak password policies on some accounts, attackers were able to crack the password hashes and obtain legitimate account access.
2. Issue Tracking System Information Leak: After obtaining initial access, researchers further infiltrated the contractor's issue tracking system. This system stored sensitive configuration data for the automaker's telematics infrastructure, including user credentials and password hash files for the in-vehicle telematics server, providing a critical stepping stone for subsequent attacks.
3. Telematics Platform Protection Failure: On the automaker's side, firewall misconfigurations caused some internal servers to be externally exposed. Researchers used previously obtained service account credentials to successfully access the server file system, where they discovered another contractor's access credentials, enabling lateral movement and ultimately gaining complete control over the telematics system infrastructure.
4. Firmware Update Mechanism Abuse: Researchers discovered that the telematics platform could push firmware update commands to vehicles without effective integrity and authenticity verification mechanisms. Attackers could upload tampered firmware to the Telematics Control Unit (TCU) and use it to access the vehicle's CAN bus.
5. Vehicle Critical Systems Remotely Controlled: Through the CAN bus, attackers could further access critical ECUs such as the engine and transmission, enabling manipulation of core vehicle functions, including forced gear shifting or engine shutdown while the vehicle is in motion, posing a direct threat to occupant safety.

media.caption: God Mode On: Researchers run Doom on a vehicle’s head unit after remotely attacking its modem
media.credit: God Mode On: how we attacked a vehicle’s head unit modem

text.headline: Remote Breach of Vehicle Modem: Researchers Achieve "God Mode" Control Over Head Unit System
text.text:
On November 20, researchers Alexander Kozlov and Sergey Anufrienko from Kaspersky ICS CERT disclosed a high-severity vulnerability in in-vehicle communication modems that could lead to the remote complete takeover of a vehicle's infotainment system.

1. Vulnerability Discovery and Initial Intrusion (Modem Side)
Targeting the Unisoc UIS7862A SoC, researchers extracted modem firmware from the vehicle head unit's motherboard for analysis and discovered a stack overflow vulnerability (CVE-2024-39432) in the 3G RLC protocol (UM mode). This vulnerability can be triggered by a single malformed SDU packet before secure channel establishment, achieving remote code execution (RCE), directly bypassing 3G/LTE communication security mechanisms, and serving as the starting point for the entire attack chain.
2. Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement (SoC Microarchitecture Layer)
After successfully controlling the modem (CP), researchers established stable bidirectional control capabilities through ROP chains, MPU reconfiguration, and NAS protocol communication. They subsequently discovered that CP and AP share a physical memory address space, and further exploited hidden and disabled DMA peripherals to bypass software isolation mechanisms, achieving arbitrary read/write access to AP (Android/Linux) memory, completing lateral movement from the modem to the application processor.
3. Kernel-Level Control and Complete Takeover (AP Side)
With the ability to directly read and write AP memory, researchers located the Linux kernel base address and kallsyms table, disabled SELinux, tampered with the sys_call_table, replaced system call hooks with injected kernel shellcode, and ultimately executed user-mode code in kernel mode and remotely launched the Doom game. At this point, relying solely on a single modem vulnerability, the attacker could achieve "God Mode" control over the entire vehicle head unit SoC.
